 The post  Domes Resorts details Greek expansion for Casa Collective  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Following its acquisition of Casa Collective, Domes Resorts has announced three new hotel openings in Greece for 2027. The expansion will see Casa Cook debut in Halkidiki and Santorini, alongside a new Cook’s Club property in Kassandra, marking the next phase of development for the lifestyle hospitality brands. Casa Cook Athos will open in northern Greece in Summer 2027, reviving a 1959 Modernist landmark overlooking a sheltered bay on the lesser-known peninsula near the gateway to Mount Athos. Originally designed by one of Greece’s leading architects, Periklis Sakellarios, and now reimagined by Berlin-based studio Vision Alphabet, the 60-key hotel’s architectural character has been preserved through a sensitive restoration with Casa Cook’s distinctive, understated design, and will open a further 45 rooms its second stage. The hotel will comprise guestrooms, suites and a villa, two restaurants with local dishes and wines that reflect paréa, direct beach access and a spa with Yoga, breathwork, meditation and sound rituals amongst its wellness programming. The launch of Cook’s Club Kassandra marks the next evolution of the brand, introducing its first property on the Greek mainland, alongside a new creative direction. Scheduled to open in Summer 2027 among the pine-covered hills of Kriopigi on Halkidiki’s western peninsula, the adults-only property resembles a relaxed, private summer house centred around the main pool and pool bar area. The Boathouse, an open kitchen and restaurant, offers locally sourced dishes, the spa and outdoor gym are accompanied by yoga platform and the landscaped gardens provide social areas for extended relaxation. Art plays a heightened role with contemporary pieces and large murals displayed throughout the hotel, and a collaboration with Brazilian artist Luciano Cian marks the beginning of a wider series of creative partnerships, from original works and live murals to occasional artist residencies. Casa Cook Santorini will be the third property to open in 2027 in the village of Firostefani with just six traditional cave-style residences. Rooted in the island’s traditional whitewashed cave houses with striking Caldera views, the adults-only boutique hotel brings the brand’s design philosophy to a more personal scale, through tailored experiences, privacy and the flexibility to discover the island at one’s own pace. “The acquisition of Casa Collective represents an important step in our growth strategy, allowing us to expand our lifestyle ecosystem while building on the distinct identities of Casa Cook and Cook’s Club,” saidsaysDr. George P. Spanos, CEO of Domes Resorts and Chairman of Casa Collective. “These three openings in hotels we own showcase how much we believe in the soul and the character of these brands.” Remo Masala, Founder of Casa Collective and Vision Alphabet, adds: “As Casa Collective grows, we’re building on our deeper understanding of our guests to create meaningful reasons to return, with experiences that respect the individual character of each brand and destination.” casa collective Casa Cook Domes Resorts europe expansion Greece Related Posts 24 January 2025 Casa Cook to launch first mountain retreat 29 March 2023 Domes announces further Greek expansion 6 December 2021 Domes Resorts to expand internationally

items.title: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings
items.summary:
As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow […] 
 The post  Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings 5 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow and bioclimatic design can improve guest comfort while reducing energy consumption. How are changing guest expectations reshaping environmental comfort in hospitality? Rising temperatures and increasingly demanding guest expectations are making thermal comfort a strategic priority for hospitality operators. At the same time, rising energy costs are putting pressure on operating margins. The challenge is to create consistently comfortable environments without allowing energy consumption to escalate. This requires a more intelligent approach to managing temperature, airflow and insulation. What is bioclimatic architecture, and why is it so important for hotels and residences? Bioclimatic architecture considers the relationship between a building, its local climate and the people who use it. In hospitality, this means combining effective insulation, natural or mechanical ventilation and efficient heating and cooling systems to reduce reliance on air conditioning. By designing for climate from the outset, hotels can improve thermal comfort, reduce energy demand and create spaces that feel naturally comfortable while preserving their architectural identity. How can climate and airflow enhance the guest experience? Comfort is not determined by air temperature alone. Air movement influences how the body perceives heat, allowing guests to feel comfortable at higher thermostat settings. By combining air conditioning with well-designed ventilation, hotels can create a more balanced and pleasant indoor climate, while reducing energy consumption. The result is an environment that feels better, operates more efficiently and supports a more enjoyable guest experience. How do your solutions help hotels reduce energy use without compromising comfort? The key is to move beyond the assumption that lower temperatures automatically mean greater comfort. Setting air conditioning to 20°C, for example, can significantly increase energy consumption without necessarily delivering a better guest experience. By combining efficient ceiling fans with air conditioning, hotels can maintain comfort at higher thermostat settings and reduce cooling energy consumption. Based on results reported by our clients, this approach can deliver energy savings of 30–45%, depending on the building, climate and operating conditions. Our objective is to make comfort measurable, efficient and easier to manage. Can you share a hospitality project that demonstrates the impact of your approach? One Ibiza Suites is a good example of how a considered combination of building performance and airflow can transform the guest experience. By improving roof insulation and introducing ceiling fans in the lobby and restaurant, the hotel enhanced thermal comfort in key shared spaces. The combined intervention achieved a reduction in perceived temperature of approximately 4°C, demonstrating that comfort can be improved without relying exclusively on more intensive air conditioning. What’s next for Magnovent? Our next step is to help hospitality operators reduce their reliance on air conditioning, in both summer and winter, with a target of reducing energy consumption by an average of 30%. Through increasingly sophisticated control systems, we aim to manage airflow, heating and cooling as an integrated solution, helping operators maintain their desired level of perceived comfort while optimising energy use. Ultimately, we want to move the industry towards a more intelligent understanding of temperature: one in which buildings are designed and operated around how people actually experience comfort, rather than simply the number displayed on a thermostat. www.magnovent.eu air conditioning bioclimatic design climate change guest comfort magnovent Related Posts 19 September 2023 Inside FOH’s luxury hospitality solutions 22 June 2023 Madera talks timber, bespoke design and hospitality interiors 5 December 2019 Cameron Design House’s Inari chandelier designed for hospitality settings

items.title: Thompson Hotels lands in Rome
items.summary:
Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, […] 
 The post  Thompson Hotels lands in Rome  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, marking the brand’s debut in Italy . Set within a reimagined iconic landmark on Via delle Botteghe Oscure, Thompson Rome draws on the architectural character of its 1940s home and the layered history of Via delle Botteghe Oscure, one of Rome’s most significant streets and a landmark in post-war Italian political history. Original elements, including a sweeping marble staircase, have been carefully restored, while a sculptural wall and inlaid floor by celebrated Italian artist Gio Pomodoro, rediscovered during the renovation after decades hidden from view – have been preserved and given new prominence within the hotel. Bespoke furnishings, refined detailing and layered natural materials bring a contemporary expression to the building’s history. Thompson Rome’s 69 guestrooms and suites take cues from the character of a contemporary Roman residence, pairing warm natural materials with custom furnishings and understated details. With 19 suites, nearly one-third of the hotel’s accommodation offering, guests can choose from Junior Suites, Suites with patios or terraces, and the 104-square-metre Thompson Suite with 80-square-metre private terrace. Designed as a counterpoint to the energy of the city outside, the rooms feel residential and refined, with select accommodations offering views across Rome’s historic rooftops and landmarks. Several rooms feature balconies overlooking Via delle Botteghe Oscure, while select rooms offer private patios facing Rome’s historic buildings. Thompson Rome’s art programme, creates a dialogue between the history of the site and contemporary art. The collection brings together works by artists associated with the Scuola Romana and the Scuola di Piazza del Popolo, alongside contemporary artists whose practices reflect Rome’s longstanding cultural openness and international influences including Francesco Del Drago, Giangaetano Patanè, and Guido Strazza. Presented throughout the hotel’s public spaces and guestrooms, the artworks are an integral part of the guest experience, connecting the memory of the site with the creativity of Rome today. A rotating artist-in-residence programme will further extend Thompson Rome’s connection to the city’s creative community through exhibitions, conversations and other cultural programming. Three distinct food and beverage venues carry Thompson Rome from morning espresso and leisurely lunches through aperitivo, dinner and drinks above the city. At Lyve Restaurant, Executive Chef Fabio Fioravanti brings a contemporary Mediterranean approach to ingredients and traditions from the Italian coast and across the region. Seafood is central to the menu, with Mediterranean fish and shellfish alongside dishes that draw on bouillabaisse, rockfish broths, wild coastal herbs and rouille, reworked with a lighter touch while preserving the depth and character of the originals. The same attention extends to the pastry kitchen, where precise technique and contrasting flavours and textures shape the dessert menu. A native of Ostia, Fioravanti brings more than two decades of international experience, including time with the Alain Ducasse group and at the three-Michelin-starred Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse at the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo. At Lyve, that technical precision carries through a dining experience that is refined yet relaxed, with the quality of the ingredients and clarity of the cooking taking centre stage. Above the hotel, Lyve Rooftop pairs views across Rome with cocktails, Italian aperitivi and a menu designed for sharing. The Lobby Lounge offers the hotel’s most casual gathering place throughout the day, from coffee and light fare to aperitivo and cocktails. The hotel will extend the guest experience through a year-round programme shaped by Rome’s culinary, artistic and creative communities. Experiences will range from culinary workshops and guided tastings to Empire of Light, a photography-led experience from the hotel’s seventh floor that invites guests to discover Rome from above. “Rome has such a strong identity, so we wanted Thompson Rome to start with the city itself,” says Amar Lalvani, Chief Creative Officer, Hyatt Corporation and President & Creative Director, The Lifestyle Group, Hyatt . “The building, the neighbourhood, the food, the people and the way Romans live all shaped the hotel. The goal was to create a Thompson hotel that feels at home in Rome, a hotel travellers want to discover and Romans want to come back to.” architecture europe hotel design hyatt interior design italy rome thompson hotels Related Posts 14 June 2023 Thompson Hotels heading to Rome 21 February 2022 Design Hotels welcomes four new members 9 August 2021 Thompson Hotels arrives in Savannah

Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab […] 
 The post  Capella to open at Dubai Peninsula in 2030  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Capella Hotel Group has announced Capella Dubai, set to open in 2030 on the Dubai Peninsula in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The 115-key hotel will include a collection of suites with private pools, culminating in a 600m 2 Capella Suite conceived as a residential-style retreat. Set along one of Jumeirah’s most desired shorelines, Capella Dubai will open within the 210-acre waterfront destination by H&H. Conceived as a first-of-its-kind, design-driven destination, the Dubai Peninsula brings together hotel brands and private residences, complemented by dining, retail, a superyacht marina, a kilometre of private beach and over two million square feet of botanical gardens. Developed by H&H and designed by Denniston , the hotel will feature five social venues from the lobby lounge and The Living Room to the signature restaurant. Above it all, the rooftop will be home to a specialty restaurant and destination bar, inviting guests to dine against the Dubai skyline. Stretching nearly 70m across the rooftop, the pool will offer a tranquil retreat above the city, alongside single and double cabanas. A family pool will also feature at beach level. Capella Wellness will offer a holistic approach to wellbeing, encompassing the Auriga Spa, a Fitness Centre and Mind Body Studio, as well as an outdoor fitness area. Inspired by the restorative rhythms of the moon, Auriga Spa will feature male and female treatment rooms, a co-ed suite and VIP suite, alongside a hammam, hydrotherapy circuit pool, two biohacking facilities and grooming services. Dedicated relaxation lounges will offer quiet spaces to pause before and after treatments. For celebrations and gatherings, Capella Dubai will offer a spacious ballroom with a pre-function lounge, complemented by two meeting rooms, a VIP Majlis and an outdoor event lawn. “As Capella grows beyond Asia Pacific into the Middle East and Europe, we are entering an important new chapter for the brand,” says Roland Fasel, President, Capella Hotel Group. “The Middle East shares our appreciation for craftsmanship, culture and exceptional service, making it a natural home for Capella. Capella has always been deliberately selective about where it goes, choosing destinations where we believe we can create something meaningful and distinctive. “At Dubai Peninsula, our partnership with H&H is the foundation for all that we are building. They share our vision for the intimate, highly personalised experience Capella is known for, one that connects guests more deeply with Dubai, its culture and its people. With the opening of Capella Dubai in 2030, we will further establish our presence in one of the region’s most compelling cities, while remaining true to the hospitality that defines Capella.” Shahab Lutfi, Chairman, H&H adds: “Dubai Peninsula is conceived as a destination with a distinct identity, bringing together some of the world’s most renowned hospitality brands, exceptional residences and a unique waterfront setting. Capella brings a different dimension to this vision through its intimate, highly personalised approach to hospitality. We see a strong alignment between Capella’s emphasis on individual experiences and sense of place and our ambition to create a destination that offers more than exceptional design and location. Capella Dubai will introduce a more intimate, service-led hospitality experience to the city’s resort landscape, adding depth and character to the overall offering. “Working alongside Denniston, we are bringing hospitality, architecture and landscape together from the outset, ensuring that each responds to the setting and contributes to a coherent vision. For us, the strength of Dubai Peninsula lies in the way its different elements come together, from its shoreline and central park to its collection of hospitality and residential offerings. Capella’s distinctive character will be an important part of that mix, shaping a destination that feels considered, cohesive and different.” capella capella dubai Denniston dubai dubai peninsula H&H Jumeirah Related Posts 27 August 2025 Mandarin Oriental to open second Dubai outpost 11 October 2024 Ennismore’s Delano lands in Dubai 9 December 2009 Dusit Princess debuts in Dubai

items.title: Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel
items.summary:
The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the […] 
 The post  Spagnulo & Partners redesigns Milan Marriott Hotel  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: The historic Milan Marriott Hotel has entered a new chapter following an extensive interior renovation by Spagnulo & Partners, the Milan-based architecture and interior design studio led by Federico Spagnulo, Alessandra Carbone and Andrea Spagnulo. Encompassing the hotel’s 317 guest rooms, public areas and event spaces, the project establishes a contemporary architectural language that draws on the property’s history and its longstanding relationship with the city. The project is guided by a principle of architectural continuity, expressed through a system of geometries, proportions and materials that evolves across the interiors according to their scale and function. The grid emerges as a recurring design element, first appearing in the full-height shelving that structures the public areas before becoming a graphic motif reinterpreted in handwoven rugs and textiles. As it shifts in scale and material, its precise geometry takes on a softer, more tactile expression. In the communal areas, the design creates a sequence of spaces with different degrees of openness and intimacy. Bespoke furnishings define the various areas while maintaining visual continuity, whereas the use of wood introduces a warm, tactile element that balances the rigour of the geometry. The predominantly neutral colour palette is punctuated by carefully chosen colour accents, provided by upholstered furniture and rugs, which help to characterise the spaces and create different atmospheres. The same attention to proportion and the guest experience informs the renovation of the 317 guest rooms, where clean lines, natural finishes and contemporary furnishings create interiors conceived around comfort and functionality. The design responds to the requirements of international hospitality, balancing practical considerations with material quality and a distinctive visual identity. From the organisation of the spaces to the design of the furnishings and the lighting scheme, the project embodies Spagnulo & Partners’ bespoke approach, rooted in the relationship between architecture, materials and the quality of living. The result is a hotel that reinvents its character through a restrained design language, capable of interpreting the demands of contemporary hospitality whilst maintaining a connection with its history. hotel renovation italy Marriott milan renovation Spagnulo & Partners Related Posts 27 September 2023 Marriott International launches new midscale brand 9 May 2023 W Hotels to debut in Milan 27 July 2015 First-ever Marriott Hotel in Makkah

items.summary:
Hilton has announced the opening of Casa Verbena Madrid, Outset Collection by Hilton, an intimate 45-room hotel on Calle de […] 
 The post  Hilton opens Europe’s first Outset Collection hotel  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Hilton has announced the opening of Casa Verbena Madrid, Outset Collection by Hilton, an intimate 45-room hotel on Calle de Preciados in the heart of the capital. Marking the first Outset Collection hotel in Europe, the hotel features interiors by Madrid-born designer Lorenzo Castillo, complemented by views across the city’s rooftops. Casa Verbena Madrid takes its name from the traditional Spanish verbena: a lively neighbourhood celebration that brings people together through food, music and shared traditions. The hotel also draws on costumbrismo, the Spanish artistic tradition of depicting local customs, characters and daily rituals, looking beyond the capital’s landmarks to the cafés, streets and squares that shape life for Madrileños. The hotel’s interiors reflect a distinctly local perspective on the city. Costumbrismo-inspired artwork, warm materials, fluted glass, brass finishes and layered textures reference Madrid’s architectural and cultural heritage in a contemporary way. Many guestrooms look onto Preciados street and its typical Madrid façades, while Preciados Rooms open onto terraces with views across the city’s rooftops and towards the Royal Palace. “Casa Verbena Madrid offers a fresh perspective on the capital, whether guests are discovering it for the first time or returning to experience it differently,” says Álvaro Mazaheri, Managing Director, Arte Hoteles. “From a breakfast inspired by local favourites to recommendations we would share with friends, we want each stay to reveal more of the Madrid that lies beyond its best-known sights.” Elizabeth Scruggs, Brand Leader, Outset Collection by Hilton, also comments: “Casa Verbena Madrid represents the essence of Outset Collection, offering guests a stay that feels deeply connected to the destination. As our first hotel in Europe, it sets the tone for how we envision the collection growing around the world: through independent hotels with compelling stories, strong local identities and a genuine sense of discovery. With more than 100 hotels under development globally, we are building a collection of individual hotels that invite travellers to experience a destination through a more personal lens, all with the benefits of Hilton.” David Kelly, senior vice president, Continental Europe, Hilton, concludes: “Madrid is a special destination for Hilton, and in recent years we’ve broadened our presence in the city with distinctive brands and properties designed to meet different traveller needs. Casa Verbena Madrid builds on that story as the European debut of Outset Collection by Hilton. Full of character and with a strong sense of place, the hotel reflects the creativity and energy of Madrid. items.title: First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos
items.summary:
Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, […] 
 The post  First Look: Andaz Turks & Caicos  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Andaz has unveiled a first look at the interiors for Andaz Turks & Caicos. Set to open in Spring 2027, the property will mark the first Hyatt hotel in Turks & Caicos and the first Caribbean island resort for the Andaz brand. The 132-key resort is designed by architecture by RAD Architecture with interiors by Modus Operandi in collaboration with Hyatt. Gently curving with the coastline, the west-facing property will offer a sunset perspective at every touchpoint. Set directly on the white sands of Grace Bay and steps from Bight Reef within Princess Alexandra National Park, Andaz Turks & Caicos will comprise 59 hotel rooms and 73 branded residences, also available for stays, with 10 penthouses featuring their very own rooftop plunge pools. The resort will feature three swimming pools, the 7,000ft 2 Runa Spa & Wellness, four dining concepts, a dedicated Kids Club, tennis and pickleball courts, in addition to ample weddings and event space. The structural narrative of Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay will unfold around an arrival sequence that takes cues from the island’s early history, when visitors arrived exclusively by boat. The entrance will recreate this experience, translating the pier into a long, immersive progression toward Grace Bay. Guests will move along a wood-lined corridor whose framing references the skeleton of an overturned boat. Set 15ft above the sea, the vantage point will immediately give the feeling of floating over the water as panoramic ocean views open up. That connection will continue throughout the interiors, where local stone and rich, natural materials add warmth while shifting hues of blues draw the surrounding waters indoors. The guestrooms’ expansive views and indoor-outdoor living will be balanced by a sense of privacy. Teak and hardwoods, richly textured fabrics and streams of natural light filtering into the bathrooms will create a tactile warmth, while artwork by Caribbean artists and pops of colour will bring the island’s character indoors. A traditional Turks & Caicos dress, distinguished by its colourful stripes representing the individual islands, will serve as a cultural touchpoint for the interiors. The striped pattern is reinterpreted in the wooden headboards, translating a recognisable element of local dress into a subtle design detail. In addition to 59 standard guestrooms, the 73 branded residences include studios as well as one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom layouts, with the largest four-bedroom residences spanning up to 8,336ft 2 of indoor and outdoor space. Each residence will offer a balcony or terrace, indoor-outdoor living spaces and a Bosch-equipped kitchen. Natural woods, textured fabrics and contemporary furnishings are paired with handcrafted pieces and Caribbean-inspired graphics, creating a warm, layered interior palette. Ten penthouses will feature private rooftop plunge pools, while select residences offer private pools. Anchoring the resort’s social scene, the lobby bar is inspired by the colourful homes found throughout the Caribbean. Saturated hues, natural materials and an open-air setting will create a relaxed, residential feel, while the bar’s expansive setting will make the landscape part of the backdrop. As one of Grace Bay’s only indoor-outdoor oceanfront restaurants, Tamarà’s interiors will feature deep bottle-green tile to evoke the lushness of a tropical forest, balanced by limestone tiling and natural materials. A fishnet-inspired canopy will shade the expansive outdoor terrace, where a central tree will be framed by cascading lights that echo the movement of leaves overhead. Baie will unfold across two levels beside the pool, with the upper level offering a lounge-like perch above the water. The laidback sanctuary will serve as a casual pool bar by day, shifting into a more refined setting with sunset rituals in the evening. Adjacent to the lobby, Palmette will blur the line between neighbourhood café and marketplace, pairing daytime fare with a considered edit of locally made goods including baskets, clothing, tableware, candles and other provisions. The coastline also informs Runa Spa & Wellness, where the calm of Grace Bay’s reef-protected shallows finds expression across natural woods, neutral tones and sculptural forms punctuated by pops of colour that reflect the bay’s shifting hues of blue. The resort’s fitness centre will complement the spa with Life Fitness equipment throughout. items.title: Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma
items.summary:
Experimental has announced the opening of its new Roman address, a vibrant and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary […] 
 The post  Rodolphe Parente envisions Experimental Roma  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Experimental has announced the opening of its new Roman address, a vibrant and cinematic hotel designed to embody a contemporary Dolce Vita. Located on the Via Veneto in a building that formerly housed a bank, the hotel features 82 rooms, a rooftop, a suspended swimming pool, and an interior scheme by Rodolphe Parente. “For Experimental Roma, I did not want to recreate or imitate a nostalgic vision of Rome,” says Parente. “Instead, I wanted to create a living tribute, a free interpretation expressed through materials and space. A place charged with the same tensions that define Rome itself: sacred and profane, splendour and decadence.” In the lobby, the designer has curated an intimate interior that blends heritage and reinvention. Italian opulence is revisited through a French lens and the legacies of great Italian masters – such as Gio Ponti, Carlo Scarpa and Luigi Caccia Dominioni – are referenced through subtle nods to the 1970s: chrome tubing, disco-inspired accents, lurex carpets, a sculptural staircase and rich and textured materials. Throughout the restaurant and public spaces, enveloping banquettes, quilted drapery and exposed beams pay homage to Italian cinema, while the rooftop features an expansive bar overlooking the Eternal City, a swimming pool and a terrace. The hotel’s 82 rooms are divided into two principal categories. The first evokes the theatrical Roman bedroom, bathed in light filtered through interior shutters. Large blocks of colour, dramatic headboards inspired by antique drapery and a sense of romantic intimacy reminiscent of Villa Medici define these spaces. Colourful basins, vibrant details and a richer, more expressive design language create a dialogue between ancient Roman baroque influences and the hedonism of the 1970s. The second category embraces a more refined, almost futuristic aesthetic. Mineral patinas, two-tone lacquered ceilings and ribbed stainless-steel headboards resembling contemporary sculptures create a contemplative atmosphere. Artworks throughout the rooms evoke the worlds of Cy Twombly, Christo, Ugo Ferranti and the Yvon Lambert Gallery. The bathrooms are conceived as contrasting boxes, balancing warm wood with cool stone, raw materials with bespoke graphic details. “Experimental Roma is a hotel of inverted perspectives,” Parente concludes. “A French interpretation of Italy; an Italy reinvented through materials, textures and light. Noble materials interact with reimagined industrial elements. Marble converses with folded stainless steel, while terracotta tones vibrate against polished metal surfaces. Rome is reflected – quite literally – as if in a mirror. It is a city of shadows and reflections, a city that never exhausts itself, that continues to inspire dreams, desire and thought. This is the Rome we invite our guests to inhabit.” experimental experimental roma italy rome rudolphe Parente Related Posts 1 November 2023 Experimental Group shares first look at three new European hotels 22 September 2023 Inside Cowley Manor Experimental 20 March 2023 Experimental Group unveils Ibiza redesign

items.text: [FEATURED] BALZAR ARQUITECTOS RESTORES 1890S RESIDENCE IN HISTORIC VALENCIA Located in the historic center of Valencia, Spain , Ciutat Vella Apartment is an interior renovation by Balzar Arquitectos set within an 1890 residential building. Sited in an urban context characterized by layered historical traces, the project approaches preservation not as a static museum display, but as an active framework for contemporary domestic life. Original architectural elements, including geometric Nolla mosaic tile floors, wrought ironwork, decorative ceiling moldings, solid timber doors, and surviving polychrome wall fragments, were retained and restored to guide the layout and spatial rhythm. all images ©David Zarzoso RESTORED MOSAICS AND LIME PLASTER ANCHOR WABI-SABI MATERIALITY Guided by a wabi-sabi philosophy prioritizing material patina and natural imperfection, the intervention by Balzar Architectural Studio introduces a restrained palette of lime plaster, unfilled travertine, solid wood, linen, and wool. Surface textures take precedence over color, complemented by diffused daylight filtering through historic apertures. The interior blends vintage pieces sourced from Nekonato Gallery with artworks from CLC Arte, custom site-specific joinery by Balzar Arquitectos, and contemporary furnishings, including seating by New Works and luminaires by Venicem, establishing a balanced conversation between 19th-century craft and modern minimalism. items.text: [FEATURED] STUDIO RUEI designs hybrid AUTOMOTIVE GALLERY and CAFÉ IN WAN CHAI Designed by Yuisze Wong of Studio Ruei, Macchina is a hybrid gallery café in Hong Kong’s Wan Chai district that integrates automotive exhibition spaces with hospitality programming. Framing vehicles as cultural and industrial artifacts rather than commercial commodities, the interior provides a social venue where automotive design, mechanical engineering, and specialty coffee converge. all images ©matte is the new black CONCRETE, BRUSHED METAL, AND TIMBER FORM INDUSTRIAL INTERIOR Behind a restrained street-facing envelope, expansive glazed apertures create direct sightlines into the main display bay, framing a single vehicle as the focal sculpture, inaugurated by the Aston Martin Valkyrie. Studio Ruei organizes the internal layout and circulation through calibrated visual corridors, connecting the central vehicular plinth to surrounding lounge seating, curated display cases, and the primary espresso bar. Rotating vehicular displays introduce distinct engineering narratives over time without requiring physical alterations to the surrounding architecture. Macchina is a hybrid automotive gallery and café designed by Studio Ruei in Wan Chai, Hong Kong ADAPTABLE CEILING lights AND ACOUSTIC PANELs BALANCE AMBIANCE Drawing from Brutalist precedents, the spatial enclosure utilizes a tactile palette of textured concrete, brushed metal, and natural timber, pairing industrial finishes with precise architectural reveals that reflect automotive manufacturing tolerances. Overhead, an integrated ceiling grid pairs diffused wash lighting with directional spotlighting to delineate vehicle surfaces and contours under studio-grade illumination. Recessed acoustic panels across the walls and ceiling temper reverberation, balancing acoustic comfort across the café with the focused atmosphere of an exhibition gallery. the exhibition space displays an Aston Martin Valkyrie as a central sculptural centerpiece the minimalist service counter utilizes clean horizontal planes to minimize distraction from the exhibits custom shelving units display curated literature, automotive models, and design objects low lounge seating arrangements allow visitors to observe vehicle profiles from varied eye levels the interior design avoids conventional showroom aesthetics in favor of a gallery and café environment minimalist specialty coffee service counter features sleek metal finishes and espresso equipment a lounge area with timber elements balances the cool tones of concrete and exposed metalwork 1/10 project info: name: Macchina designer: Studio Ruei | @studio_ruei location: Gloucester Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong area: 2150 sqft photographer: matte is the new black | @matteisthenewblack designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. items.title: Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25 Years with Steinbeisser
items.summary: For its 25th anniversary, Houston Center for Contemporary Craft partnered with Steinbeisser for an experimental dinner where artist-made tableware challenged the conventions of dining
items.text: Art Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25 Years with Steinbeisser Each month, TJ Girard explores the intersection of food and design, from what we eat to how it’s made, presented, and experienced, in her Taste column. 11.06.26 | By TJ Girard Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow Steinbeisser's Experimental Gastronomy dinner at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft brought together artist-made tableware and plant-based cuisine to celebrate the institution's 25th anniversary. Photography by Kerrisa Treanor; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. I’ve covered Steinbeisser in this column before, and the Amsterdam studio’s approach to rethinking objects and how we use them continues to hold my interest. Its latest chapter took place on Oct. 23 at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft (HCCC) , where 50 guests sat together at a single long table in the main gallery, surrounded by the exhibition A Material Inheritance , to celebrate the institution’s 25th anniversary. Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s 25th-anniversary experimental dinner in collaboration with Steinbeisser. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Founded in 2009 by Jouw Wijnsma and Martin Kullik, Steinbeisser launched its Experimental Gastronomy initiative in 2012, pairing chefs and artists for one-of-a-kind dinners worldwide. This was its first in Texas and one of the few held in the U.S. The menu was entirely plant-based and seasonal, with produce from regional farms that use organic and biodynamic growing practices. The cooking came from two Michelin-starred restaurants: Tatemó in Houston and Nicosi in San Antonio. The evening opened with Bohyun Yoon’s Singing Buoys , an interactive work in which guests used handheld remotes to steer blown-glass vessels carrying small bites across a water table. When the vessels collided, they rang like bells. Guests interact with ‘Singing Buoys,’ an interactive sonic installation by artist Bohyun Yoon, created for the amuse-bouche at the Steinbeisser dinner. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. The dinner itself kept the focus on the objects. Tatemó’s first course of nixtamalized squash, rice, kosho, and carrot came on Jaydan Moore’s Sustenance #1, a platter assembled from salvaged antique silver-plated serving pieces. The first course featured nixtamalized squash, Koshihikari rice, kosho, and carrot, served on Sustenance #1 by Jaydan Moore, a sculptural platter assembled from reclaimed antique silver-plated servingware. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Nicosi’s Kudzumochi Tamal, with pumpkin juice, mushroom, masa foam, hoja santa, and gold leaf, was prepared by chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm. Chefs Jorge Luis Hernández and Ben Hjelm of Nicosi plate the second course. Photography by Jenny Antill; courtesy of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. The course arrived on Adam Knoche’s Exploding Plate, made from crushed basalt clay pressed and fired at 2,250 degrees Fahrenheit to intentionally fracture, alongside his carafe and sauce bowl made from foraged Texas clay and Galveston shells.   Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets  
 Jess Miles .
items.text: Weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets WORDS BY Jess Miles November 9, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Inside the factory: weaving narrative and a sense of place with Ulster Carpets Editor of SPACE, Jess Miles, travels to Portadown to see how Ulster Carpets makes bespoke carpets for the world’s most revered hospitality projects, from package dyeing and patented looms to a design studio that weaves a property’s story into every pile… After a long, hot summer, it was a welcome change look out at the verdant landscape of Northern Ireland, just hours after leaving the heat-beaten brown of the Sussex countryside. Admiring nature’s enduring carpet seemed a fitting start to the day, before soon arriving at Ulster Carpets in Portadown to take a first-hand look at the craftsmanship behind the luxury carpets made for some of the most acclaimed hospitality projects in the world. Although it has now grown into a global business with clients and projects of grand scale, Ulster has manufactured on this small-town site since it was founded in 1938, and today keeps all of the process in-house across three UK sites. Dyeing, weaving, inspection, finishing and despatch all take place here in Portadown, where around 95% of Ulster’s carpet is made. The remainder is produced at a second site in Northumberland, while wool is spun first at Ulster Yarns, the company’s mill in Yorkshire. Now a fourth-generation, family-owned company, Ulster remains centred on the people, skills and expertise that have been continually refined over generations of designers, weavers and makers. Image credits: Ulster Carpets Ulster’s commitment to its Northern Irish roots is evident upon arrival, where I’m greeted by the close-knit team who show me around with buckets of passion for the work they do. Among them was Ciara Halligan, Marine Sales Manager, who started out at Ulster as a weaver over 30 years ago. Now she works with clients, drawing on her specialist knowledge to show them the endless possibilities of what Ulster can achieve. But Ciara, it turned out, was no exception. As the tour went on, I realised everyone I met had either spent years at the company or had followed in family members footsteps there. It is a heritage Ulster carries with pride, built on investment in its people and, as I would soon see, its engineering and machinery too. First stop was the Dyehouse and Energy Centre, which has transformed dyeing at Ulster in terms of both time and sustainability. Gone are the old-school hanks of yarn immersed in huge dye baths. Instead, yarn is wound onto perforated tubes, and the dye is circulated through it – a method known as package dyeing. Heat from used water is recovered to warm fresh water drawn from an on-site borehole, and since the centre opened in 2018, water consumption has fallen by 46%. Better still, the dye penetrates the wool more deeply, giving richer colours. Image credit: Ulster Carpets The dyehouse is also home to Ulster’s colour hub, with a bank of over 9,000 colours to draw on. My eyes light up like a magpie to gold when the drawers of tufted colour samples are pulled open, but if none of these are the exact shade needed, a bespoke match can be developed from a client’s material or colour reference. From there, we – and the yarn – head to the looms. There are 40 Axminster looms in all, each running Ulster’s patented PSYLO weaving technology which allows for up to 25 colours within a single design, creating more intricate concepts full of texture, movement and depth. I also got to see a new generation of looms in action, engineered and built in Sunderland by GTM (a company within the Ulster Group), designed to produce more carpet using less energy per square metre. It was quite the experience standing in the room as the factory floor boomed to the beat of the looms – and watching the many cones of coloured yarn being drawn in and woven into the finished design was nothing short of a visual feast. Onward, every inch of every carpet is then visually inspected, with any mending painstakingly done by hand. Before despatch, each order is rolled out side by side to check the pattern lines up across adjoining rolls. Having walked through the end-to-end physical process, I was struck by how meticulous the craft of making carpet is, and I certainly left with a newfound appreciation for it. But what surprisingly captured my attention most was my final stop – the design studio. Image credit: Ulster Carpets There, Senior Designer Sarah Moffatt showed me the concept for Ulster’s stand at an upcoming trade show. Working to the theme “designed to be remembered”, the team looked to their Northern Irish heritage, drawing on the patina of the local landscape. They photographed corroded metal around the factory and the nearby beaten chalk landscape, then zoomed in on the textures and patterns until they became abstract forms. Warm tones of rust and weathering supplied the base colour palette, with different shades used to create tonal depth and dimension. It was an insightful illustration of how Ulster approaches its custom work, which makes up the majority of its hospitality projects. Rather than working from existing collections, the team designs bespoke carpet for each property and the individual areas within it, working closely with the interior designer or client to weave the wider narrative of the project into the carpet itself. Storytelling is always a big part of the brief, and Moffatt explained how the team might research a property’s history, from the cultural background right down to its local plant life. On one heritage project, the leaf veining of native plant species was translated into a carpet through colour and form. Image credit: Ulster Carpets The team’s creative skills also extend to technical problem-solving. One

items.text: Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 • Hotel Designs Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 9, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Fairmont New Orleans: Fairmont Hotels & Resorts hits 100 Fairmont Hotels & Resorts has offically opened Fairmont New Orleans, marking the much-anticipated return of the brand to the Crescent City after two decades – and marking Fairmont’s 100th hotel globally… Developed by Kailas Companies and operated by Fairmont Hotels & Resorts , Fairmont New Orleans occupies 17 stories of the former Bank of New Orleans building, a 31-story landmark originally designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in 1970. Its original sidewalks, entry canopy, lobby floors and concrete walls on the first and second floors have been fully restored and refurbished, alongside the second floor’s decorative bronze paneling and local cypress ceiling. Rather than looking primarily to the French Quarter’s colonial architecture, the property draws inspiration from the glamour and optimism of the 1970s, celebrating an often-overlooked chapter in New Orleans’ architectural evolution. Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Omer Acar, CEO, Fairmont Hotels & Resorts, said: “Celebrating Fairmont’s landmark 100th hotel in New Orleans is a moment of perfect alignment. This is a city built on the very poetry of celebration, culture, and hospitality, setting the ultimate stage for such a historic milestone. After two decades away, returning to New Orleans feels like a joyful homecoming. This magnificent property is designed to be a vibrant social epicenter, a sanctuary where the city’s rich heritage meets a sophisticated, contemporary energy. Through meticulous design, spirited gastronomy, and exceptional spaces created for connection, we are not just opening a hotel; we are welcoming the soulful spirit of New Orleans back into the global Fairmont family for our next great chapter.” Interior design by Rockwell Group explores the contrasts that define New Orleans, imagining a city emerging from a verdant landscape and shaped by generations of cultural influences from around the world. Mid-century references nod to the decadence of the 1970s oil boom era, while layered textures, saturated colour, local flora, and globally influenced patterns bring a contemporary interpretation of New Orleans design, balancing old and new, polished and playful, and vibrant and restful. Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas The hotel’s lobby serves as its social anchor and a cultural living room designed to welcome both visitors and New Orleanians throughout the day. Guests arrive beneath a mirror-clad monumental stair that reflects a three-story magnolia flower and Spanish moss-inspired chandelier. Custom brass relief panels from Italy frame the check-in and concierge desks, while the Lobby Bar pairs handmade Italian lava-stone tiles with a floor mosaic composed of six marbles in a distinctly 1970s pattern. The Lobby Bar’s cocktail-focused beverage program and live entertainment encourage guests and locals to linger from day into evening. “Today marks an exciting new chapter for Fairmont New Orleans and for our city,” said Eric Overstreet, General Manager, Fairmont New Orleans. “From the moment guests enter our lobby to an evening at Delmonico Steakhouse, the hotel was designed to feel distinctly of New Orleans, while offering the service and experience Fairmont is known for. We’re proud to welcome travelers and our local community into these spaces and look forward to seeing Fairmont New Orleans become part of the city’s next chapter.” Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Fairmont New Orleans’ 250 guest rooms and suites are conceived as personal retreats with residential warmth, eclectic finishes, curated furnishings and layered materials designed to feel collected over time. Three-dimensional entry mosaics reference classical European flooring, while large, panelled artworks evoke the rich flora of Louisiana’s bayous. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame sweeping city views, while custom artwork and details reference the cultural and natural history of New Orleans. In select king rooms, ‘faux balconies’ with café tables offer a playful nod to the city’s beloved porches and terraces. Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Delmonico Steakhouse marks the celebrated concept’s debut in New Orleans and its first location outside of Las Vegas, bringing Chef Lagasse’s grand American steakhouse to the city that has long inspired his culinary career. Open for dinner, the restaurant pairs timeless steakhouse traditions with his signature bold New Orleans flavours. Open for breakfast and lunch, The Café by Emeril offers a more relaxed brasserie-style experience, combining French-inspired classics with Creole accents and Southern influences. From chicory-laced coffee to thoughtfully prepared breakfast and lunch favorites, the café flows seamlessly into the lobby, creating an inviting gathering place for hotel guests and locals alike. “I’m thrilled to bring Delmonico Steakhouse to New Orleans alongside The Café by Emeril, creating two distinct dining experiences that reflect what I love about cooking and bringing people together,” said Chef Emeril Lagasse. “We’re proud to be a part of Fairmont’s return to the city and look forward to welcoming both locals and visitors to experience the bold flavors, genuine hospitality, and unmistakable New Orleans spirit that defines everything we do.” Image credit: Fairmont New Orleans / Matias Vargas Forthcoming dining and drinking venues, set to open in early December also, include the property’s rooftop pool and Bleu Perdu, along with Third Measure cocktail bar. With the masks on from doors-opening, here are the official photographs from Hotel Designs’ most unforgettable event yet… Continuing the legacy of The Brit List Awards , the 2026 edition celebrated a decade of championing the best in British and international hotel design and hospitality. Last night, on 5th November, London’s iconic Ministry of Sound opened its doors to the industry’s most creative and influential figures, who traded their usual attire for masks, glamour and a little mystery. Presided over by Hotel Designs Publisher Katy Phillips, Editor Sophie Harper and SPACE Editor Jess Miles ( also the stars of this year’s teaser video ), the evening transformed the venue into a theatrical world of opulence. The night’s headline moment came with the unveiling of the 15 award winners, chosen from more than 250 finalists. Winners were invited to the stage to be crowned and receive their specially designed trophies from EGGER. Also revealed on the evening, The Brit List 2026 book profiles the top 75 interior designers, architects and hoteliers redefining British hospitality. The full list and digital guide are available to explore below. None of this would have been possible without the support and creativity of our incredible sponsors, so here’s a look at the brands who helped make the tenth Brit List Awards a night to remember. Balsan returned as our red carpet partner, unveiling a 2026 entrance carpet in theme of the masquerade. The French carpet specialist has a heritage stretching back almost three centuries. Muraspec joined Informare as event partners, providing 8-foot pieces of masquerade artwork. The wallcovering brand has been designing and manufacturing in the UK since the 1850s. Schlüter-Systems celebrated with us once again as photobooth partner, the company’s 12,000-plus products can be found at Lympstone Manor, The Newt and Raffles at The OWO. Phillip Jeffries was the award partner for The Interior Designer of the Year Award. Our showcase partners brought the glamour: ADA Cosmetics returned for a second year, sending guests home with their signature goody bags filled with Lalique creams, perfumes and body washes. Amtico was back for a second year. The British luxury vinyl tile specialist has been perfecting its craft since the early 1960s. GROHE joined as a first-time sponsor and, as promised, the team were firmly planted on the dancefloor. Hypnos returned with its much-loved super king bed installation near the stage. Every Hypnos mattress is handcrafted in Buckinghamshire, and the brand has been perfecting sleep for more than 120 years. EGGER , our trophy partner, crafted this year’s winners’ trophies from sustainably sourced wood, a lasting reminder of each winner’s accolade. Finally, thank you to Bonfire , who captured the mood, the wins and the dance moves as our videographers for the evening. items.title: Designed to last: the future of hotel design
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Designed to last: the future of hotel design  
  Designed to last: the future of hotel design  
 Sophie Harper .
items.text: Designed to last: the future of hotel design Designed to last: the future of hotel design WORDS BY Sophie Harper November 6, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Designed to last: the future of hotel design At the Egger Showroom in Clerkenwell during London Design Festival, a panel of hospitality design specialists gathered to ask a deceptively simple question: how do you design a hotel that outlasts the moment it was made for? Chaired by Hotel Designs’ Editor Sophie Harper, the discussion brought together Despina Kalapoda of Marriott International, Sarah Williams of Goddard Littlefair and textile designer Emma Shipley . Their answers differed in detail but converged on one idea: what endures is rarely what shouts loudest. For Despina Kalapoda, longevity begins with discipline. Each Marriott brand rests on fixed principles drawn from who its guest is, with room left for local character. “These are things that each brand needs to remain true to,” she said, giving design a thread that survives every change of fashion. The same logic applies to sustainability: build a solid base, refresh the soft finishes, and question whether anything truly needs replacing. In Barcelona, one hotel was obliged to tile over its bathrooms rather than create waste. Considering sustainability at the development stage, she added, is “way more efficient” than waiting for the next renovation. Image credit: Egger Sarah Williams carried the thought from brand to place. A narrative rooted in landscape, architecture and local culture does not date, she argued, because “That’s not based on trend. That is based on the true DNA of the place.” Even the trickiest brief, a space that serves coffee by morning and cocktails by night, is best solved not by compromise but by invention, with people as part of the performance. At the Corinthia London, for example, a single display table turns afternoon tea into evening theatre. “It’s got to involve the people,” she said. Luxury, she added, has yet to embrace recyclable materials, and designers share responsibility for changing that perception. Emma Shipley, whose hand-drawn, nature-inspired collections have sold steadily since 2018, offered the human counterpoint. “Humans have always been inspired by nature, and I’m sure that will always continue, especially in this digital age we’re living in,” she said, adding that handcrafted work will only become more relevant. Textiles, she noted, are also the gentlest way to renew a room. That digital age loomed over the evening’s lightest and most revealing exchange: the humble hotel television. Despina noted waning enthusiasm for in-room screens, while Sarah admitted to a certain resentment, since the TV dictates where the bed, and therefore the view, must go. Her recent treehouse stay, watched over by an Alexa, left her wanting only to escape. Hidden technology, the panel suggested, serves the guest; visible technology too often intrudes. Image credit: Egger None of the panel claimed to know what a hotel room will look like in fifty years, but all were agreed that the answer to what makes lasting design work well lies less in any fixed features and more in how you make people feel in any given space. Build flexibly, stay distinctive, and hold on to the human connection at the heart of hospitality. Trends will pass. The feeling, if it is built well, stays.   The Landmark London reimagines its Marylebone Suites as a London apartment  
 Sienna Shipton .
items.text: The Landmark London has redesigned its 48 Marylebone Suites The Landmark London reimagines its Marylebone Suites as a London apartment WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 5, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio The Landmark London reimagines its Marylebone Suites as a London apartment A £3.8 million redesign with Alex Kravetz Design swaps hotel grandeur for a more residential feel, with marble fireplaces, bespoke bars and a palette of blues, taupe and bronze… The Landmark London has unveiled a redesigned collection of 48 Marylebone Suites, marking a new chapter for the five-star hotel. Created in collaboration with architecture studio Alex Kravetz Design (AKD), the spacious suites blend the building’s historic grandeur with a more contemporary, residential style . Image credit: The Landmark The inspiration is the feel of an elegant London apartment. Classic details are balanced with modern touches, and generous living areas, marble-framed fireplaces and bespoke bars make the suites as suited to relaxing and entertaining as to sleeping. A tranquil palette of blues, taupe and neutral shades is layered with warm bronze accents, tailored upholstery and textured wall panelling. Soft lighting runs throughout, from the expansive living rooms to the bedroom retreats, easing the move from day to evening. Image credit: The Landmark The investment, totalling £3.8 million, covers several suite styles. The 60 sqm Marylebone One Bedroom Suite has a separate living room with a statement fireplace, built-in bookcase and workspace. The Marylebone Junior Suite balances architectural detail with plush furnishings, blurring the line between hotel suite and private pied-à-terre. For families and groups, the Marylebone Family Suite pairs two double beds with a large living space and an Italian marble bathroom, with interconnecting rooms available. Amenities include Dyson hair tools, ARGENTUM toiletries, Smart TVs with Sky and a fully stocked bar with Cartwright & Butler treats. Younger guests are catered for with toys, activities and teepees on request, and a warm cookie and milk turndown at bedtime. items.title: HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal
items.summary:

 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal • Hotel Designs HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 5, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal HBA Los Angeles, the flagship studio of the award-winning global hospitality design firm, has announced the appointment of Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal… A respected designer and creative leader with more than 20 years of international experience, Gaglione brings expertise across luxury hospitality, branded residences, restaurants, and mixed-use developments. His appointment further strengthens HBA Los Angeles’ creative capabilities and positions the studio for continued growth. Gaglione joins HBA Los Angeles following more than six years of running his eponymous design practice, where he led a portfolio of hospitality and high-end residential projects defined by tailored interiors, rich materiality, and quiet confidence. His recent collaborations include projects with MGM Resorts, IHG Hotels & Resorts, and Dreamscape Companies. He previously held senior design roles at Kelly Wearstler, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and HBA Singapore. “At HBA Los Angeles, we are committed to investing in the next generation of design leadership while building upon the collaborative culture and design excellence that have long defined our studio,” said HBA Los Angeles Partner Kathleen Dauber. “Gianpiero is the right leader to help shape our next chapter. The combination of his creative vision, international experience, and proven leadership makes him exceptionally well-suited to balance creative ambition with the needs of clients and the complexity of hospitality projects.” Throughout his career, Gaglione has contributed to some of the hospitality industry’s most celebrated properties across North America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. His distinguished portfolio includes Santa Monica Proper, Downtown Los Angeles Proper, The Beekman and The Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York, Soho Beach House in Miami Beach, and Rosewood Miramar Beach in Montecito, Calif. Drawing upon his multidisciplinary background in concept development, interior architecture, FF&E design, and project management, Gaglione creates spaces that emphasize craftsmanship, distinctive character, and a strong sense of place. “HBA has an extraordinary legacy in hospitality design, and I’m excited to join the Los Angeles studio at such an important time in its evolution,” said Gaglione. “I’ve always believed the most compelling interiors are those that feel authentic, personal, and enduring rather than driven by trends. I look forward to collaborating with the talented team, bringing new ideas to the design process, and creating environments that are both memorable for guests and meaningful for our clients.” In his new role, Gaglione will help guide the studio’s creative vision, oversee design projects, and mentor emerging talent while strengthening client relationships. items.text: Accor expands Handwritten Collection through new Verdi Hotels partnership • Hotel Designs Accor expands Handwritten Collection through new Verdi Hotels partnership WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 4, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Accor expands Handwritten Collection through new Verdi Hotels partnership Accor and Corinthia Group have launched a strategic collaboration to bring Verdi Hotels to Handwritten Collection… As part of the collaboration, five Verdi hotels in Malta, Portugal and Tunisia will join the Handwritten Collection brand under a franchise agreement from November 2026, with plans to add two further properties in Hungary and the Czech Republic. Verdi Hotels was launched by IHI plc in 2024 as a distinct management platform in the upscale segment, operating independently from th e Corinthia brand , which is positioned in the luxury hotel sector. Through this new collaboration, Verdi’s management platform will benefit from Accor’s global distribution, marketing and loyalty programmes, further strengthening its performance and operating capabilities. Image credit: Verdi Gzira Promenade Designed to bring together characterful independent hotels, Handwritten Collection showcases properties defined by their strong personality and the genuine warmth of their hosts. Since its launch in 2023, the brand has rapidly grown to more than 50 curated hotels in 22 countries, and a pipeline of 58 hotels around the world. Combining the individuality of independent hospitality with the scale, distribution power and growth platform of Accor, the brand is designed to create long-term value for owners and investors. Simon Naudi, CEO of Corinthia Group, said: “We are very pleased to announce this strategic relationship with Accor. While our focus on the global growth of the Corinthia brand remains undiminished and entirely independent, the development of our second brand, Verdi, will now benefit from Accor’s extensive global marketing reach and the strength of its Handwritten Collection.” Paul Pisani, President of Verdi Hotels, added: “We are very much looking forward to this new relationship, which will add value to our Verdi Hotels and give us the opportunity to grow the brand in new and exciting destinations.” image credit: Verdi St. George’s Bay Philippe Bijaoui, Chief Development Officer, Premium, Midscale & Economy brand for Accor in Europe & North Africa, commented: “This strategic partnership with Verdi Hotels marks an important step in our continued growth ambition. By combining the strength of Verdi Hotels’ management platform with Accor’s distribution, loyalty and brand ecosystem, we aim to unlock new opportunities, accelerate growth and create sustainable value for both parties.” The initial Verdi Hotels properties that will join Handwritten Collections include: Verdi Gżira Promenade, Malta – Located on Malta’s Marsamxett Harbour waterfront, Verdi Gżira Promenade is situated along the lively Gżira seafront promenade and a thriving shopping district. The hotel is within easy reach of Malta’s principal business and leisure districts, making it a convenient base for both business and leisure travellers. Verdi St. George’s Bay Marina, Malta – Situated on St. George’s Bay in St Julian’s, the property enjoys a prominent waterfront location overlooking one of Malta’s best-known bays. The hotel is located close to vibrant dining entertainment and commercial areas, while also providing direct access to the Mediterranean coastline. Image credit: Verdi Tunis Beach Resort Verdi Dragonara (formerly Vivaldi Hotel), Malta – Verdi Dragonara looks out across the Dragonara headland toward the open sea, where the coastline turns rocky and the pace slows. It sits just beyond the busiest streets of St Julian’s, so guests enjoy calmer surroundings and stay close to the town’s dining, leisure and business addresses. Formerly the Vivaldi Hotel, Verdi Dragonara adds a new chapter to Verdi Hotels’ presence in Malta. Verdi Tunis Beach Resort, Tunisia – Nestled on the shores of the Côtes de Carthage, the resort sits along the Mediterranean coastline within easy reach of the Tunisian capital. The property combines resort facilities with proximity to the region’s cultural attractions. Verdi Santarém, Portugal – The hotel is situated in the historic city of Santarém, north of Lisbon, and is a perfect gateway to experience Portugal’s Ribatejo region. The property is positioned within a destination known for its cultural heritage, local traditions and accessibility to other destinations in Portugal. items.text: Case Study: switching off with Hypnos at The Grove • Hotel Designs Case Study: switching off with Hypnos at The Grove WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 4, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Case Study: switching off with Hypnos at The Grove Set within 300 acres of Hertfordshire countryside, The Grove offers the sense of a true country escape, withcomfort and attention to detail throughout the resort that continues into a restful night and a refreshed start to the day… The vibrant five-star resort combines 214 stylish rooms and individually designed suites with an award-winning spa, championship golf course, and distinctive restaurants. At a destination offering so many different ways to spend the day, a restful night’s sleep is essential. The Grove has partnered with Hypnos to provide the comfort expected from a five-star stay. With more than 120 years of bedmaking experience, the fifth-generation British bedmaker works closely with hospitality clients around the world, bringing together craftsmanship, comfort and considered material choices. Image credit: The Grove Hotel “At The Grove and Luxury Family Hotels, creating an exceptional guest experience is at the heart of everything we do, and a truly comfortable, restorative night’s sleep is such an important part of that. We are delighted to partner with Hypnos, whose passion for exceptional craftsmanship, comfort and responsibly sourced materials reflects the same values and high standards we hold across our hotels. It’s a partnership we’re very proud of and one that helps us give our guests the quality, comfort, and restful experience they deserve.” – Denise Newson, Group Purchasing Manager The estate balances its rich 18th-century heritage with a relaxed, contemporary personality. Accommodation spans the historic Mansion and modern West Wing, with interiors designed to make the most of the surrounding landscape. Generous windows frame views across the gardens and countryside, while natural tones, tactile fabrics and large-scale artwork give the guestrooms a warm and individual character. Image credit: The Grove Hotel The Grove’s Mansion suites blend antique and contemporary pieces with original Georgian features, including ornate fireplaces, mouldings and curved bay windows. In the West Wing, nature-inspired interiors bring the outdoors in, creating calm and welcoming spaces in which guests can relax. Beds form a natural focal point within the guestrooms. Their generous proportions and inviting presentation reinforce the sense of comfort, helping guests to switch off at the end of the day and wake feeling rested. Image credit: The Grove Hotel The relationship is founded on more than comfort. The Grove’s commitment to protecting the planet and caring for the people within it is reflected in initiatives that champion sustainability, support the local community and invest in the development and wellbeing of its team. This closely aligns with Hypnos’ own focus on people and planet, including its careful consideration of the provenance and performance of the materials used within its beds. Whether guests spend the day on the golf course, unwind at Sequoia spa, explore the woodland trails or enjoy time together in the Walled Garden, a great night’s sleep provides the foundation for the following day. Through its partnership with Hypnos, The Grove ensures that the comfort and attention to detail found throughout the resort continue into a restful night and a refreshed start to the day.  Sienna Shipton .
items.text: Nowhere Private Island opens in the Maldives Nowhere Private Island opens in the Maldives WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 4, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Nowhere Private Island opens in the Maldives The second island from .Here Baa Atoll completes a two-island concept of just nine residences, with Nowhere offering two vast residences, designed by Christopher Chua of KulörGroup, to be reserved as one private world… .Here Baa Atoll Maldives has announced the opening of Nowhere Private Island, the second private island of .Here. It completes a two-island concept that redefines ultra-luxury hospitality in the Maldives through scale, silence and space. Located within the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve of Baa Atoll, Nowhere joins Somewhere, which opened in December 2025, to realise .Here’s vision of luxury defined not by excess, but by presence. The two islands comprise just nine private residences, creating one of the smallest and most exclusive resort offerings in the Maldives. Somewhere was conceived for gathering, connection and shared experience. Nowhere is a more secluded expression of the concept: an entire private island devoted to only two residences, designed to be reserved as a single, fully private world. Together they embody .Here’s “Art of Duality” concept, the freedom to embrace vibrant connection or complete seclusion, to do everything at once or nothing at all. Image credit: .here Maldives Nowhere is home to two residences defined by generous scale and complete privacy. The five-bedroom Presidential Residence spans more than 25,800 square feet, while the three-bedroom Overwater Residence offers over 10,000 square feet of living space. The island is designed for fully self-contained living, with a private cinema, fitness studio, steam and sauna facilities, and the exclusive Fehi Wellness couples treatment room. At the heart of Nowhere is a philosophy of quiet grandeur. Singapore-based architect Christopher Chua of KulörGroup has created expansive volumes, refined proportions and uninterrupted horizons, with architecture expressed through clarity and restraint so that the landscape becomes the focal point. Interiors by Inge Moore and Muza Lab draw on natural materials, soft tonal palettes and layered textures inspired by the surroundings. Environmental responsibility has informed the development from the outset. Material selection, building placement and architectural scale were guided by a commitment to preserving the island’s ecosystem, with every design decision made to enhance rather than overwhelm the natural environment. Image credit: .here Maldives Guests have access to SAFAR, .Here’s signature overwater restaurant, where Executive Chef Georgios Vasilopoulos presents a world-influenced menu centred on fresh seafood, seasonal produce and fire-led cooking from the Josper Grill. At SAFAR Bar, handcrafted cocktails draw on journeys, spices and distant destinations. Bespoke private dining can be arranged on secluded sandbanks, private terraces or within each residence, and every stay includes 24-hour in-residence dining supported by a dedicated private chef and mixology service. Fehi Wellness on Nowhere offers bespoke treatments and personalised wellness programmes, with a couples treatment room and yoga chamber accessible only to those staying on the island. Service is anchored by a dedicated one-to-one Roohu butler. Although designed around complete seclusion, .Here remains connected to the wider destination. Guests on either island enjoy complimentary access to every dining venue, wellness offering and experience at sister resort Finolhu, a Seaside Collection Resort, combining total privacy with the energy and variety of a full-scale luxury resort. items.title: Heritage design at The Connaught: the art of appearing unchanged
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Heritage design at The Connaught: the art of appearing unchanged  
  Heritage design at The Connaught: the art of appearing unchanged  
 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: Heritage design at The Connaught: the art of appearing unchanged • Hotel Designs Heritage design at The Connaught: the art of appearing unchanged WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 3, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Heritage design at The Connaught: the art of appearing unchanged At The Connaught, heritage is not treated as a fixed moment in time. For almost two decades, Guy Oliver has guided the evolution of one of London’s most recognisable hotel interiors, ensuring that each new chapter feels entirely at home within the building… Dating back to the late nineteenth century in this location (although the hotel dates back to 1812), The Connaught has an identity shaped over generations. Oliver has worked closely with Ulster Carpets to create bespoke designs for both public and private areas of the hotel. In public areas, carpet can become a defining focal point. The design on the grand staircase establishes a strong rhythm across the treads and landings. Viewed from above, it emphasises the scale and structure of this important space, while its rich colour palette complements the surrounding timber. Elsewhere, in corridors and on the staircase serving the private events spaces, a monochrome pattern draws the eye through the connecting areas. Although very different in character, both designs demonstrate how pattern can reinforce the architecture rather than simply decorate it. Image credit: The Connaught Hotel Oliver’s recent work includes the restoration of The Connaught’s rooms and suites. Traditional mouldings, crafted cabinetry, artwork and carefully considered textiles establish a connection with the building’s past. Bespoke carpets designed by Oliver and made by Ulster contribute to the ambience without distracting from the architectural detail. Organic designs in blue and green soften the formality of the rooms, helping the interiors feel comfortable and residential while retaining the grandeur of The Connaught. Image credit: The Connaught Hotel “The Connaught has such a strong identity that any new chapter must maintain continuity with the past, weaving a timeless story that feels ‘ever thus’ while remaining current and contemporary. Every element of the hotel is bespoke, and the carpets are a big part of that, bringing colour, comfort and character to a space. Working with Ulster Carpets, I developed designs tailored to each setting, from quiet tonal schemes in guestrooms to bolder patterns on staircases and in corridors. Whatever the setting, the carpet must also meet the practical demands of a working hotel.” – Guy Oliver, Oliver Laws The contrast between these spaces shows how carefully carpet must be designed for its setting. In a guestroom, it contributes to a calm atmosphere and provides acoustic and physical comfort. In corridors and on staircases, it must work from multiple viewpoints, maintain the integrity of its pattern and withstand constant use. Image credit: The Connaught Hotel Ulster Carpets’ bespoke design and manufacturing capabilities give Oliver the freedom to tailor his carpet designs to each setting while maintaining the quality and performance required throughout the hotel. Interiors must evolve over time to respond to the changing needs of guests and the operation of the hotel. At The Connaught, perhaps the greatest compliment is that the result appears to have been there all along.
