 Sienna Shipton .
items.text: Raffles The Red Sea opens on Shura Island Raffles The Red Sea opens on Shura Island WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 3, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Raffles The Red Sea opens on Shura Island Raffles’ first Red Sea resort, part of Foster + Partners’ Coral Bloom masterplan, pairs butler service and residential-style villas with destination-led dining, restorative wellbeing and a dedicated cultural curator… Raffles Hotels & Resorts has announced the debut of Raffles The Red Sea . Set between a lagoon and the open sea on the northwestern shores of Shura Island, with expansive views across the Red Sea, the resort follows the contours of the island. It offers a new way to experience Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea through design, dining, culture and the intuitive service for which Raffles is known. “The opening of Raffles The Red Sea marks an exciting new chapter for Raffles in Saudi Arabia,” said Omer Acar, CEO, Raffles Hotels & Resorts. “Set within one of the world’s most remarkable marine environments, the resort brings the distinctive character of Raffles to a new and compelling destination in the Kingdom. From highly personalised service, delivered through the intuitive care of our butlers, to the comfort and privacy of residential-style accommodations, every element is designed to create a stay that is both inspiring and unmistakably Raffles. As we continue to expand across Saudi Arabia, this opening reflects our ambition to create exceptional hospitality experiences in extraordinary destinations, building on the legacy of legendary service and enchanted glamour that have defined Raffles for nearly 140 years.” Image credit: Raffles Hotels & Resorts Part of Foster + Partners ’ Coral Bloom masterplan, conceived to enhance Shura Island’s natural state, the resort is designed around a close relationship with the water. Light-filled interiors, layered textures and coastal tones draw the surrounding landscape indoors, while terraces, pathways and gardens lead the eye towards the lagoon and open sea. The resort comprises 121 guestrooms, 14 suites and 33 private pool villas, an intimate collection of accommodations that gives couples, families and multigenerational groups room to experience the island at their own pace. Guestrooms open onto private terraces with lagoon or sea views, while suites offer generous indoor-outdoor living with expansive terraces oriented towards the surrounding waters. Guests in every room, suite and villa will enjoy Raffles’ legendary Butler Service, which anticipates their needs and creates unexpected moments of magic. Raffles Spa & Wellness and the adults’ pool will be unveiled in a future phase. Designed as a place to pause between the island’s more active moments, the spa will include seven treatment rooms, a hammam, sauna and steam facilities, a vitality pool and an outdoor lap pool. In-room and private rituals will be available for guests who prefer greater privacy. In the meantime, guests can enjoy the gym, padel and water sports. Image credit: Raffles Hotels & Resorts The connection to place continues through cultural programming led by a dedicated Raffles Curator. Encounters with local art, literature, storytelling and craftsmanship offer different ways into the region’s living culture. The children’s and teens’ centres, which offer age-specific opportunities to explore, play and create, will open at a later stage. The Curator’s Room will provide an intimate setting for gatherings, celebrations and cultural exchange. “Our aim is to give guests the freedom to find their own rhythm on the island,” said Charles Saliba, Managing Director, Raffles The Red Sea and Fairmont The Red Sea. “A day might begin on the water, move into the spa, end over dinner by the sea, or unfold more quietly through art, storytelling and time together. The experience is designed to feel personal, unhurried, and connected to the place.” Image credit: Raffles Hotel & Resort Shura Island extends the possibilities of each stay. Guests can spend a morning at Shura Links, Saudi Arabia’s first 18-hole island golf course, explore the marina, discover Marina Village and the island’s dining and retail, or take to the coast through WAMA water sports and Galaxea diving and marine discovery. Akun offers land-based activities, while the island’s beaches invite a slower pace. The destination reflects a regenerative tourism approach, with the development designed to work in close relationship with the island’s natural environment. Powered entirely by renewable energy, Shura Island is reached from Red Sea International Airport by electric vehicle across the 3.3-kilometre Shura crossing. items.text: Tom Ravenscroft Editor-in-chief 26 September 2026 This week on Dezeen , we revealed the architecture, interiors and design projects in the running to win this year’s Dezeen Awards . Over the week, we announced all the projects shortlisted for this year’s awards, starting with the 152 projects in the running for the 19 architecture project categories on Monday . On Tuesday, we revealed the 112 shortlisted projects in the 14 different interiors project categories before unveiling the shortlisted design projects on Wednesday. Bentley revealed its first electric car this week In London, car brand Bentley revealed its first fully electric car – an SUV named the Torcal. Ahead of its unveiling, we spoke to design director Robin Page about how the car aims to embrace heritage in a “progressive way”. Bugatti unveiled plans for a skyscraper in Miami In the USA, car brand Bugatti revealed plans to build a 60-storey skyscraper in Miami , which would be its first branded residence in the US. Designed by US architecture studio Brandon Haw Architecture with interiors by Yabu Pushelberg , the skyscraper would join other developments by luxury car brands Porsche , Bentley , Mercedes-Benz and Aston Martin in the city. Meta showcased its Muse Charm device At the Meta Connect showcase, the tech company revealed a series of new products including two new pairs of smart glasses . The company also debuted its Muse Charm device , which is a tamagotchi-style AI agent. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” said Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you.” A Peter Zumthor gallery was one of this week’s most popular projects The most popular projects on Dezeen this week include a trio of buildings for a Swiss museum by Peter Zumthor , a charred timber-clad home in Japan , a multi-generational house in Bengaluru . Listen to our journalists talk about the key design and architecture stories of the past seven days on our Dezeen Weekly podcast , which this week focused on Apple’s folding phone. The shortlist also features a nightclub with a “layered and atmospheric” interior in the UK, a villa with rocks dramatically suspended over its staircases in Greece and a storehouse-turned-futuristic hair salon , also in the UK. items.summary:
Fifteen leading architects and designers met last week to decide the winners of Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, which will be revealed at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party in November. The master jury took place at the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel in London and included architects Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind as well […]

items.text: Chater Paul Jordan 17 September 2026 Fifteen leading architects and designers met last week to decide the winners of Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble , which will be revealed at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party in November. The master jury took place at the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel in London and included architects Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind as well as interior designers Wendy Saunders and Jaime Hayon . Designers Martin Lotti and Jo Barnard , as well as architects Dominique Petit-Frère and Aziza Chaouni also joined to determine the 49 winning projects, ahead of next week’s shortlist announcements between 21-23 September. Winners announced at the Royal Opera House All this year’s winners will be announced at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party which takes place at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November. Guests at the party will be the first to find out who has won the prestigious project of the year awards across architecture, interiors and design. Tickets are available to purchase here . Also unveiled at the ceremony will be the six winners of this year’s Designers of the Year, who have each been shortlisted and selected by Dezeen’s editorial team. The Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design. “Designers thinking more critically about context” The master jury discussed 392 shortlisted entries selected from over 4,300 projects in 91 countries around the globe. Architectural designer John Cummins joined the architecture master jury panel which comprised architects Yansong , Libeskind , Chaouni and Petit-Frère . Speaking to Dezeen, Petit-Frère observed how “this year’s projects reflect a generation of designers thinking more critically about context, materiality, technology, and the social impact of what they create”. Top image: (from left to right) John Cummins, Dominique Petit-Frère, Daniel Libeskind, Ma Yansong and Aziza Chaouni. Above: (from left to right) Wendy Saunders, Jaime Hayon, Smita Thomas, Benni Allan and Julien Sebban at the master jury day at One Hundred Shoreditch Hayon and Saunders were joined on the interiors master jury panel by Benni Allan , Julien Sebban and Bangalore-based Smita Thomas . Thomas was also struck by the depth of this year’s entries, which she saw as imbued with a sense of purpose rather than being solely aesthetic exercises. “There were a number of projects that felt more like statements of intent than displays of style,” she said. “It charged me to see design beginning to shapeshift toward strengthening human connection in a time when we need it most,” Thomas continued. Parisian designer Sebban noted the “presence of so many young and emerging studios experimenting with new materials and new ways of thinking”. “The next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers” Lotti and Barnard were alongside Michael Anastassiades , Min Chen and Alexie Sommer to decide the winners of the design categories. Lotti, chief design officer at sportswear brand Nike , remarked that “the strongest projects weren’t simply beautiful – they were purposeful, distinct and challenging the status quo”. “What struck me most was the range of thinking behind it. I came away feeling that the next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers,” he continued. (From left to right) Alexie Sommer, Min Chen, Michael Anastassiades, Jo Barnard and Martin Lotti at the master jury day in London Following the day of judging, an exclusive drinks reception and dinner took place in the One Hundred Room at One Hundred Shoreditch, where the master jury was joined by fellow 2026 judges Zandra Rhodes and Miminat Shodeinde . Designers Paul Cocksedge , Ron Arad and Sebastian Cox also joined to celebrate the day’s conclusion. Following the shortlist announcements next week, the Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote will open and readers will be asked to vote for their favourite shortlisted projects. We will announce the public vote winners on Dezeen and across our social media channels ahead of the Dezeen Awards party on 16 November. Zandra Rhodes and Paul Cocksedge joined for the celebratory dinner at One Hundred Shoreditch. Photo by Olivia Chenery Tickets for the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are on sale. The occasion is an opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work. Studios that have been shortlisted for this year’s Dezeen Awards will be eligible to purchase discounted tickets for £249. These tickets will be released on 21 September, alongside the shortlist announcements. Subscribe to the Dezeen Awards newsletter to keep up to date with the latest announcements on the party. items.text: Emma Gaukroger 2 June 2026 Interior designer Corey Damen Jenkins and designer Mark Grattan have joined the judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026. Dezeen Awards, in partnership with Trimble , is searching for the world’s best architecture, interiors and design. Hurry, the late entry deadline closes tomorrow! Submit your projects by 23:59 London time on Wednesday 3 June for the chance to put your work in front of our panel of industry-leading judges. Read on to find out more about who will be judging this year’s entries: Corey Damen Jenkins will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors jury Jenkins, principal and chief executive officer of Corey Damen Jenkins & Associates, will judge this year’s interiors entries. The New York City -based interior design and architecture practice is internationally celebrated for its approach to layering colours, textures and patterns to create timeless and tasteful spaces. In addition to his work across residential and hospitality projects, Jenkins has produced expansive product collections for home furnishings brands including Kravet , Hancock & Moore , Maitland-Smith and Eichholtz . Mark Grattan will judge this year’s design entries Grattan, a multidisciplinary designer based in New York City , will join the design jury alongside Natasha Jen and Gustaf Westman . Grattan’s practice spans furniture, interiors, textiles and objects and is underpinned by a strong focus on materiality. The designer’s work is housed in the permanent collections of the Brooklyn Museum and the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture . items.text: Emma Gaukroger 25 May 2026 Interior designer Julien Sebban , graphic designer Natasha Jen , creative director Gabriella Khalil and architectural designer John Cummins have joined the judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026 . Dezeen Awards, in partnership with Trimble , is searching for the world’s best architecture, interiors and design. Hurry, entries close in less than three days! Submit your projects by this coming Wednesday 27 May at 23:59 London time. Read on to find out more about who will be judging this year’s entries: Julien Sebban will join this year’s interiors panel Sebban is the founder and creative director of Paris -based multidisciplinary design collective Uchronia . He brings his signature bold and joyful approach to immersive projects spanning restaurants, retail spaces, private residences, boutique hotels and monumental installations. Sebban’s practice aims to blur the boundaries between architecture, interior design, scenography and collectible furniture. Recent projects include a hotel suite with an underwater feel , a playful installation at Coachella and a psychedelic revamp of a womenswear boutique . In 2023, Uchronia was named Dezeen Awards emerging interior designer of the year . Natasha Jen will judge this year’s design entries Jen is a multidisciplinary designer and partner at the global branding studio Pentagram . The New York -based graphic designer’s work explores the overlap between technology, contemporary culture and the built environment through graphic identity across physical and digital contexts. Jen has worked on projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Harvard GSD , as well as architecture practices BIG , OMA and Weiss/Manfredi . An internationally recognised and acclaimed practitioner, she was awarded an honorary fellowship by the Royal College of Arts for her contributions and achievements in the industry. Gabriella Khalil will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors jury Khalil is a creative director, designer and curator known for her immersive approach to design, hospitality and cultural programming. She is the co-founder of Palm Heights , Grand Cayman’s first boutique hotel, and is the creative director at WSA, a New York City -based workspace and event hub. Khalil aims to merge beauty, cultural resonance and human connection in her work, creating spaces that feel both elevated and deeply connected. John Cummins will judge Dezeen Awards 2026 Cummins is an architectural designer and product marketing manager at 3D modelling software brand Trimble SketchUp . He advocates for technology-as-facilitator to help build space for designers to spend time on the human decisions to create meaningful and inspiring built environments. Drawing on his architectural experience, the designer now works closely with some of the largest architecture, engineering and construction firms around the world to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings. items.text: Emma Gaukroger 22 May 2026 Architects Sharon Johnston , Kulapat Yantrasast and Ben Cross have joined the judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026 alongside designer Alexie Sommer . Dezeen Awards, in partnership with Trimble , is searching for the world’s best architecture, interiors and design. Hurry, entries close next week! Submit your projects by 23:59 London time on Wednesday 27 May for the chance to put your work in front of our stellar panel of industry-leading judges. Read on to find out more about who will be judging this year’s entries: Sharon Johnston is a founding partner of Johnston Marklee Johnston, a founding partner of Los Angeles -based firm Johnston Marklee , will judge this year’s architecture entries. The firm’s recent projects include a green-metal tower in Phoenix , a lakeside guesthouse in Upstate New York and the conversion of a historic Los Angeles car showroom into an art gallery . Beyond practising architecture, Johnston has taught at universities including the Harvard Graduate School of Design , Princeton University and the University of Toronto . Together with her studio partner Mark Lee, she was also artistic director of the 2017 Chicago Architecture Biennial . Kulapat Yantrasast will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture jury Joining Johnston on this year’s architecture jury is architect Yantrasast, founder of Los Angeles -based WHY Architecture . Yantrasast is known for his work on projects in the cultural realm, designing spaces that focus on the human impact of the arts. Landmark projects include an overhaul of the Michael C Rockefeller Wing at The Met , an “immersive” tent for the first Frieze Los Angeles and a museum expansion featuring a corrugated metal facade . The architect is also a board member of the Pulitzer Arts Foundation and the Noguchi Museum in New York and serves as principal architect for New Delhi’s Yuge Yugeen Bharat national museum. Ben Cross will judge this year’s architecture entries Cross, co-founder of London -based development management and advisory firm More, will join Johnston and Yantrasast on the architecture jury. At More, Cross aims to bring a design-led approach to real estate with a focus on commercial refurbishments across central London. The architect has worked across some of the UK’s most well-known commercial buildings, including No 1 Poultry , the Heal’s Building and 50 George Street. Alexie Sommer will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 design jury Sommer, a designer and communication expert who focuses on business sustainability, will judge this year’s design entries. Sommer is co-founder of Urge Collective , a climate-focused brand consultancy that helps businesses and leaders drive sustainability agendas. She also organised the Design Declares initiative, a campaign to help UK designers tackle their environmental footprint. Writing for Dezeen, Sommer argued that declaring a climate emergency is “just the beginning of the journey” . Entries close next week! There is less than one week left to enter Dezeen Awards 2026. items.text: NYC Restaurant Openings Bar Cosme From Enrique Olvera Opens Tomorrow With a Focus on Tortillas The restaurant in the former Atla space opens with fresh-pressed tortillas and cocktails from an Eleven Madison Park veteran by Melissa McCart Nov 9, 2026, 10:08 PM UTC Facebook Link Beet tiradito, lamb chops, and broccolini. | Victoria Martinez Melissa McCart is the lead editor of the Northeast region with more than 20 years of experience as a reporter, critic, editor, and cookbook author. Facebook Link While Enrique Olvera closed Atla in May, he didn’t give up the space: In its place, on Tuesday, November 10, the chef behind Cosme and Mexico City’s Pujol opens Bar Cosme at 11 Great Jones Street, at Lafayette Street. The new restaurant puts cocktails and dinner at the center of the former all-day spot, with drinks from a veteran of Eleven Madison Park and Clemente Bar, and a kitchen built around fresh-pressed tortillas. The comal — the griddle used for cooking tortillas — is central to Bar Cosme. Mexico City architecture studio Taller ADG redesigned the space with stainless steel, walnut, and black granite, including a sculptural central bar. The 40 seats are arranged around the open kitchen and comal, with floor-to-ceiling windows looking onto the corner. The comal at Bar Cosme. Evan Sung/Bar Cosme The menu is organized by seafood and crudo, like oysters with jicama, lime, and charred habanero peppers; meats with dishes like lamb belly seasoned with chintextle, a Oaxacan chile paste; vegetables and sides such as a roasted onion in salsa macha; and sweets like a guava tart. Every order arrives with fresh-pressed tortillas and salsas. In addition to a la carte, there’s a prix fixe for $135, which includes seafood, meat, a side, and dessert. Agave spirits anchor the bar, alongside a selection of bourbons. The cocktail menu is divided between “de la casa,” which are variations on familiar cocktails, and “de la barra,” original drinks from the team. The Lestat combines mezcal, corn liqueur, passion fruit, and elote salt, while the Genevieve takes a savory approach to a martini with Mexican gin, blanco tequila, and mole blanco. There’s also a sparkling highball with plantain and shiso. A 50-bottle wine list includes Mexican and natural wines. Four cocktails: Highball, Genevieve, Silas, and Lestat Victoria Martinez/Bar Cosme The drinks were developed by Sebastian Tollius and Jorsand Diaz. Tollius spent seven years at Eleven Madison Park and helped launch its upstairs Clemente Bar in 2024. Jorsand Diaz, who started as a Cosme bartender, is now the beverage director for the restaurant’s parent group, Casamata . Olvera opened Cosme in Flatiron in 2014 with Daniela Soto-Innes leading the kitchen, establishing a New York destination for contemporary Mexican cooking. In 2017, Cosme debuted on the World’s 50 Best Restaurants list at No. 40, joining Olvera’s Pujol in the top 50. That same year, the pair opened Atla, a more casual restaurant where diners could stop in for breakfast, aguachiles, or a lobster burrito. She left the group in 2020. The shift to Bar Cosme follows nearly nine years of Atla, since it opened in 2017. It became a neighborhood fixture and a comparatively less expensive introduction to Olvera’s cooking than Cosme, earning two stars from then- New York Times critic Pete Wells. Former Eater critic Ryan Sutton was a regular, too: “I’ve probably been back to Atla more than any other restaurant I’ve reviewed in the past year,” he wrote in 2018. Bar Cosme will be open nightly from 5 p.m. to midnight, with reservations through Resy for seatings from 5 to 9 p.m. Limited seating is held for walk-ins. Bar Cosme 372 Lafayette Street, New York, New York 10012, United States Link https://www.instagram.com/barcosmenyc/ See More : NYC Restaurant Openings

items.text: NYC Restaurant News A Behemoth Conveyor Belt Sushi Restaurant Descends Upon Times Square ﻿Sushiro touches down in America this month by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 9, 2026, 7:43 PM UTC Facebook Link A Sushiro in Tokyo. Bloomberg via Getty Images Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. Japan’s popular conveyor belt sushi restaurant, Sushiro , is making its American debut in New York City on Thursday, November 19, in Times Square at 667 Eighth Avenue, at West 42nd Street. Sushiro is all about kaiten sushi, aka affordable sushi rolling around on a conveyor belt. Guests at booths place their orders on a giant digital screen, and items from nigiri to tempura to ramen to desserts to sake get delivered to their tables through an intricate conveyor belt system winding throughout the space. Expect to pay $5 to $6 for most sushi pieces, and anywhere from $8 to $10 for fancier ones. People can also earn prizes by playing digital games at their tables. The New York City restaurant is huge, at 9,000 square feet. The first two floors feature 146 seats for a la carte conveyor belt dining. The lower cellar floor is dedicated to private group dining for reservations only with prix fixe menus. Sushiro started in Osaka in 1984 and grew to over 1,000 restaurants around the world under its parent group, Food & Life Companies. New York’s other Japan-based conveyor sushi belt chain, Kura Sushi, operates a location out in Flushing. Sushiro’s New York hours are from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily. items.summary: An alum of notable New York City Persian restaurants like Sofreh and Eyval is opening up his own fast-casual restaurant dedicated to Persian wraps. Chef Soroosh Golbabae is opening Āzar in Williamsburg at 740 Driggs Avenue, at South Second Street, on Saturday, November 7.  Golbabae is focusing on the idea of loghmeh, a Persian word […]
items.text: NYC Restaurant News A Sofreh Alum Showcases Persian Wraps in Brooklyn ﻿Chef Soroosh Golbabae debuts Āzar in Williamsburg this weekend by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 6, 2026, 6:35 PM UTC Facebook Link Noah Fecks Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. An alum of notable New York City Persian restaurants like Sofreh and Eyval is opening up his own fast-casual restaurant dedicated to Persian wraps. Chef Soroosh Golbabae is opening Āzar in Williamsburg at 740 Driggs Avenue, at South Second Street, on Saturday, November 7. Golbabae is focusing on the idea of loghmeh, a Persian word that means “morsel” or “perfect bite.” He explains, “Loghmeh is a super-easy homey concept that never made it out of the home,” and he’s doing something about that. To that end, Āzar is serving lavash flatbread wraps with Persian fillings that aren’t overly huge. His version of the Iranian home dining staple ghormeh sabzi ($12) is made with beef cheeks instead of the typical lamb. “Beef cheeks are a favorite cut, and it’s really hot right now, so let’s try it,” he says. It’s cooked in a herby stew with kidney beans and black limes, “until the herbs are really incorporated with all that meat flavor,” he adds, and is garnished with fresh white onions. The food spread at Āzar. Noah Fecks Soroosh Golbabae at Āzar. Noah Fecks Then there’s the koobideh ($12), with a mixture of grilled ground lamb and beef made with saffron butter, plus sumac onions, grilled tomatoes, and fresh basil. The chicken fesenjoon ($9) will be on the menu through the spring; it’s a bright filling with a pomegranate-walnut sauce, grilled chicken thighs, and pickled red cabbage. The vegetarian option is the kashk bademjoon ($9) — a “super-comforting eggplant dish,” he says. “To me, it’s the umami of Persian cuisine.” It’s made with a slow-cooked eggplant, kashk (Persian whey) , and crispy onions. He made his own lavash recipe with some whole wheat flour to add structure, as well as butter “to make it more delicious, more aromatic, and, when it reheats or holds the food, it adds a little more strength.” It’s baked in the on-site pita oven. Golbabae had been working on the idea for some time; “ Āzar is on the back burner, cooking for a long time,” he tells Eater. He knew the name from the beginning, after his mother. He grew up in Tehran, watching his mother shop and cook. “I had that education growing up without even understanding it in the beginning,” he says. The zereshk tanchin at Āzar. Noah Fecks The doogh drink at Āzar. Noah Fecks Look for sides like the tahchin ($8), a smaller take on the iconic Persian rice dish. He shares that he’s generally particular about tahchin. For this one, he went for a “softer, jasmine-like rice; we overcook it intentionally to get a little mushy,” he says. It gets seasoned with yogurt, egg yolks, saffron, and salt “so it becomes really nice and moist and fatty — kind of sticky.” While it’s typically stuffed with meat, vegetables, or barberries, he opted to serve it with the zereshk sauce (made with barberries and prunes) and pistachios for that cold-hot temperature combination. “Two things I really like to play with when I’m coming up with dishes are temperature and texture,” he says. “If you can get a few things in one bite, it’s just amazing; it’s a unique experience.” Drinks include saffron sharbat ($5), made with basil seeds and lime (“super-refreshing, he describes); and doogh ($5), the yogurt drink with dry mint and rose that gets steeped overnight. Growing up in Tehran, Golbabae frequented local street carts, kebab shops, and restaurants, and eventually worked at a few places. He worked there for a bit, and then moved to New York City to attend the Culinary Institute of America, but he wanted to go back to learning more about Persian cuisine. “I started digging [into all the old Persian recipes, thinking about how we can do that, how we can dress it in a different way that New York likes and also not lose the authenticity of it,” he says. That’s when he ended up on the opening team of Prospect Heights restaurant Sofreh (which opened in 2018) and Bushwick’s Eyval ; and then he was the opening chef and chef de cuisine of Park Slope Lebanese restaurant Sawa . He also ran Persian pop-ups and worked as a private chef. All the while, he knew that the Persian community was looking for restaurants that were more accessible and affordable. “In a lot of restaurants nowadays, in many different cuisines, they are inspired by street food, but by the time the food goes on the table, to me, it’s not anymore because they played with it too much — I’m guilty myself — but I was like, maybe this is the time to take a little risk and come out of that comfort zone,” he explains. He met Fardad Zabetian, who founded Kudo , a live-translation program, during a pop-up, and they teamed up to open Āzar. Āzar’s dining room. Noah Fecks Āzar’s exterior. Noah Fecks The 350-square-foot counter-service space is small, with only 10 seats. It’s designed by architecture firm Roudiani.Harelson . Golbabae talks about how the firm’s co-founder, Bahar Roudiani, immediately understood his Iranian architectural references because she lived in Iran. He’d ask her about old houses in Iran and stainless steel details in the Albanian sandwich shops, and she knew them all. For Āzar, that means a stainless steel counter and amber glass blocks. The walls feature artwork by fellow Iranians and Iranian Americans. Sina Choopani, who runs Tehran-based silk-screen print studio Garage.co , has some silk prints up. Zeynab Izadyar, the founder of Vvork Vvork Vvork , has patched-together quilts. Tierney Plumb is an editor of Eater’s Northeast region, covering D.C., Boston, Philly, and New York. This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in November 2026. This list will be updated weekly (see: October , September , August , July , June , May , April , March , February , January ), serving as a round-up of the dining and drinking places that have shuttered around the city. If a restaurant or bar has closed in your neighborhood, let us know at ny@eater.com. November 6 Spotlight Dumbo : After three years, Bark Barbecue will close its first-ever permanent outpost inside Brooklyn’s Time Out Market on Saturday, November 7. “All good things must come to an end,” its cowboy hat-wearing pitmaster Ruben Santana tells followers in a video message near his walk-up food hall stall. But luckily, fans of his Central Texan barbecue with Dominican touches don’t have to go far to find white oak-smoked brisket, ribs, pulled pork, and plenty of sides. Bark’s huge Bushwick location, complete with 1,000-gallon smokers, opened this summer to much excitement. Bark originally got its start as a pop-up in Queens in 2020 and grew a fan base from there. 55 Water Street, near Dock Street And the rest… East Village : La Linea , the longstanding bar and lounge known for its rotating DJ nights, watch parties for everything from the World Cup to the Knicks playoffs, and happy hour rum punches, shut down right after Halloween after a 32-year run. However, the space will get a new tenant soon. Per EV Grieve , there’s a recently approved application for a to-be-named tavern to slide in and take over. The new owners have affiliations with now-closed McKenna’s Pub and the Mayfly. 15 First Avenue, between First Street and Second Street Midtown : That was quick: Osaka, Japan-based omurice-slinging restaurant Dearbros already closed its nine-day-old pop-up at Japanese cafe BentOn on Thursday, October 29, because they were overwhelmed with guests. Looks like Crown Heights Portuguese bakery Lisbonata is opening a spinoff location focused on its soft serve , Sofi , in the West Village, at 31 Carmine Street, between Bedford and Bleecker streets. Eater has reached out for more information. Why a chef left a hyped art museum restaurant The New Museum’s new restaurant Oberon opened in July on the Lower East Side, by the Oberon Group (which runs places like Rhodora , June , and Rucola ) with co-executive chefs artist Julia Sherman and Ali Ghriskey. But then, less than a month later, Sherman left the operation. In her Substack newsletter, Salad for President , on Friday, October 30, she explained what happened behind the paywall, calling it an “ultimate failure to launch.” She recounts how the owner told her, “food doesn’t matter,” and that she wasn’t supposed to talk about the restaurant in the press. An omurice pop-up shutter That was quick: Osaka, Japan-based omurice-slinging restaurant Dearbros already closed its nine-day-old pop-up at Japanese cafe BentOn on Thursday, October 29, because they were overwhelmed with guests. They’re turning their attention to opening a permanent New York City restaurant. Eater has reached out for more information. A ramen restaurant returns One of Brooklyn’s earlier ramen slingers, Chuko Ramen , closed its 15-year-old Prospect Heights location over the summer. But it turns out the team is reopening the restaurant on the border of Clinton Hill and Bed-Stuy at 395 Classon Avenue, at Greene Avenue, in January 2027. New NYC food and drink book alerts First, Ayesha Nurdjaja , the chef and partner behind NYC restaurants Shuka and Shukette , published her first cookbook, Mediterranean All the Way . And then, drinks-focused writer Robert Simonson ’s latest, Bourbon & Rye Cocktails . “Music for a pizza restaurant” Harry Styles ended his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden at the end of October, and he celebrated with food, of course. For his final show on Halloween, aka Harryween, he dressed up as a full-on pizza rat, a reference to his first-night banter about how much he loves grabbing a late-night slice when he’s in NYC, and switched to the rat ears and a white shirt declaring “I am a rat.” That’s when he and his band ate pizza from Williamsburg Pizza on stage, per Yes Williamsburg . Continuing the theme, his girlfriend, Zoë Kravitz, dressed up as a plastic takeout bag . “I just wanna taste it” Earlier during the residency, Styles celebrated the birthday of one of his fans at the show with a cake from East Village bakery From Lucie . Political dining out NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani spent his Halloween touring the final night of the Queens Night Market with New York City Governor Kathy Hochul, who had been up for reelection that week and won. Learn about an acclaimed winemaker There’s a new documentary about renowned California winemaker Randall Grahm from director Jeffrey Reiner and producer Darin Bresnitz coming out this fall called The Terroirist . They’re hosting a preview screening on Monday, November 9, at the Loft at City Winery in Chelsea starting at 7 p.m., with a discussion between Grahm, Reiner, and moderator/winemaker/sommelier André Hueston Mack, plus wines from Grahm’s vineyard, for $36. The documentary premieres on streaming services such as Apple TV and Amazon Prime on Friday, November 13. items.text: Dining Reports This Revived Brooklyn Restaurant Serves the Best Spaghetti and Meatballs Sam’s might have a new owner, but it remains a classic﻿ by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 4, 2026, 6:37 PM UTC Facebook Link The spaghetti and meatballs at Sam’s. Nadia Chaudhury Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Sam’s isn’t a new restaurant for New York City. The neighborhood institution has been around since 1930 and has been passed down through the same family for generations. That is, until recently, when the then-owner, Louis Migliaccio, handed his legacy restaurant over to a regular, Georgia Fulton, a longtime server at the neighboring Long Island Bar . Fulton reopened Sam’s this past September, keeping its original ethos alive but in a slightly zhuzhed-up way. There’s now a much shorter food and drinks menu, still full of familiar hits. Looks-wise, the facade is unchanged, with the American and Italian flags; neon signage declaring there’s Italian cuisine, lunch, and dinner; and a couple of steps down to the front door. Inside, it’s mostly the same, but now there’s more dining room, and the front bar has actual stools. But still, familiar favorites remain, like the pizza on the menu, those same plates and glasses , and the cozy, family-friendly vibes. What to order Shrimp cocktails had been on my mind, and the one at Sam’s ($18) is a classic one with an ever-so-slightly spicy sauce with four shrimp. I had heard a lot about Sam’s baked clams ($23), and I liked them. The bivalves were chewy but tricky to pull off the shell; a little fork would’ve been nice. I adored the buttery sauce and wished I ordered bread to sop it up. The spaghetti and meatballs ($26) were some of the best I’ve ever had. It’s the ideal format, doused in Parmesan, paired with a nice zesty tomato, soft-strong meatballs, and chewy pasta. I ended with the tiramisu ($12), a classic square cut out of what is probably a huge slab of the Italian dessert with a double-ladyfinger layer. The facade of Sam’s. Nadia Chaudhury The drinks Given Fulton’s background, the drinks are quite classic and good at Sam’s. I adored my very-dirty gin martini with three olives. For dessert, my server recommended the Amaro Montenegro, which was perfectly not sweet and paired well with the tiramisu. Best seat in the house The booths are cozy and good for groups up to four. The back room is pretty, with stained glass windows and a mural of a lush garden with spouting fountains. Sit back there at the larger table for bigger groups. Hole up at one of the bar stools for solo dining and good eavesdropping. Fulton added a drink rail separating the bar from the rest of the front dining room, much like Long Island Bar . Know before you go The upstairs bathrooms offer powdered hand soap only. Insider tip Head upstairs for relics of Sam’s past, including the nonfunctional phone booth, an amazing doll lamp, and an official Brooklyn proclamation issued in 1996 recognizing the restaurant and the Migliaccio family for their mom-and-pop business efforts. items.text: Dining Out in LA Your Los Angeles Restaurant Weekend Guide: November 6 Your handy guide on where to eat from the editors at Eater LA by Eater Staff Nov 6, 2026, 9:46 PM UTC Facebook Link Popcorn chicken. | Kat Thompson Dining Out in LA Your Los Angeles Restaurant Weekend Guide: November 6 Your handy guide on where to eat from the editors at Eater LA by Eater Staff Nov 6, 2026, 9:46 PM UTC Facebook Link Popcorn chicken. | Kat Thompson Facebook Link Every Friday, our editors compile a trusty list of recommendations to answer the most pressing of questions: “Where should I eat?” Here are four places to check out this weekend in Los Angeles. And if you need some ideas on where to drink, here’s our list of the hottest places to get cocktails in town. For a generous, soulful platter: Anjahles by Jazzy in West Adams Anjahles by Jazzy. Mona Holmes When the clocks fell backwards last weekend, I woke up in need of something savory and hopped in the car to find it. I remembered seeing an Instagram post by chef Jazzy Harvey , in which she bakes cornbread in a circular foil takeout container, cuts a hole in the center, then fills it with stewy oxtails, candied yams laced with rum, smoky collard greens, and a pile of creamy mac and cheese. The end of daylight saving time provided me an extra hour to chat with Harvey and watch a steady stream of folks arrive to try out her platter at her business Anjahles by Jazzy. Harvey has been operating her soulful Jamaican-LA pop-up since 2020 and has pretty much perfected her game. Pre-orders come with extras (free drink, priority pick up). Place an order through the Anjahles by Jazzy website , and pick up in West Adams on Sunday between noon and 3 p.m. 4976 West Adams Boulevard, West Adams, CA 90016. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For one last visit to a legendary spot: Everson Royce Bar in the Arts District Nachos from Everson Royce Bar. Kat Thompson If I were to build a perfect bar in my head, it might end up a lot like Everson Royce Bar in the Arts District. You enter a dim, elegant interior, but you can also continue out back to a shady patio with enough space to host a large rehearsal dinner (literally mine). Cocktails are thoughtful but unpretentious, the list of spirits is contained in a mysterious book, beer and wine are carefully curated, and there are micheladas in both red and green varieties. The food menu is short but has no skips; the biscuits and burgers are the best in town. ERB recalls a more optimistic time in the Arts District and in LA generally, characterized by casual extravagance and a sunny disposition: a Peak TV-era mindset. But that time is over, and ERB is leaving with it — the bar is closing on December 19 . That means we’ve only got a few too-short weeks to celebrate this local icon, sampling rare whiskeys and crushing smoky potato taquitos under the tree in the middle of the patio like it’s 2016 again. 1936 E. 7th Street, Los Angeles, CA 90021 . — Ben Mesirow, editor, Eater Travel For a feast of Taiwanese flavors: Sinbala in Arcadia Kat Thompson I’ve written about the magic of legendary Taiwanese restaurant Sinbala before . It’s been serving up plates of snappy Taiwanese sausage, hearty beef noodle soup, and comforting tomato egg for more than 20 years. The menu of this strip mall cafe is expansive, ranging from snackier bites like popcorn chicken and chewy fried fish cakes to more traditional Taiwanese fare like fried pork chop rice and stewed pork belly with preserved mustard greens. Whatever you end up ordering, save room for refreshing shaved ice that comes with a slew of topping options — including but not limited to bouncy rice cakes, custardy flan, and sweet canned lychee — and a glaze of burnt brown sugar syrup. 651 W. Duarte Road Suite F, Arcadia, CA 91007. — Kat Thompson, audience editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For a mini English breakfast near LAX: Tomat in Westchester Tomat. Matthew Kang There was a never a good answer for where to eat near LAX before a mid-day flight, until Tomat opened in nearby Westchester. The handy all-day restaurant provides a peaceful morning or mid-day meal with some interesting modern British dishes that won’t weigh you down before boarding a long flight to Asia (which I did recently). The full English breakfast, usually a bit of a gutbuster, comes in a three-quarter-size portion at Tomat, featuring farmers market potatoes, house-made pudding, comforting stewed beans (not the canned variety), and half-crispy bacon. The egg is poached instead of pan-fried, and the toast is hearty sourdough. You’ll want another dish — in our case, the pastrami hash topped with a fried egg, laden with crispy chopped potatoes and plenty of fresh herbs — to feel completely full. The fermented hot sauce adds a vibrant punch and a simmering heat that will linger. Note: Breakfast is served only Wednesday to Sunday. 6261 W. 87th Street, Los Angeles, CA, 90045. — Matthew Kang, correspondent, Eater Related The 38 Best Restaurants in Los Angeles See More : Dining Out in LA Dining Out

items.text: Dining Reports Mariscos El Muelle 8 Delivers a Sensational Taste of Culiacán in Downey The new restaurant has an expanded menu, a full liquor license, and a bright, boisterous energy by Bill Esparza Nov 6, 2026, 4:40 PM UTC Facebook Link Ceviche Muelle 8 at Mariscos El Muelle 8 Bill Esparza Bill Esparza is a James Beard award-winning food journalist, author of LA Mexicano, and onscreen food television personality covering food in United States and Latin America. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Culiacán-based Mariscos El Muelle 8 has closed its East LA food truck and upgraded to a brick-and-mortar restaurant in Downey that opened on Friday, October 30. The owner of Mariscos El Muelle 8 USA , Jay Orozco, had launched the food truck in Garden Grove in 2025 after closing a previous brick-and-mortar location of Mariscos El Muelle 8 in Downey. His new 95-seat restaurant has a full liquor license and big-screen TVs for sports events. Founded in Culiacán in 2020 by Orozco’s cousin, the late Abel Martínez, Mariscos El Muelle 8 launches its new Downey restaurant with an extensive menu of barra fría (cold bar) dishes such as ceviches, aguachiles, and seafood cocktails, as well as barra caliente (hot bar) items like seafood tacos and soups. The bright cantina is ideal for sipping margaritas, micheladas, and carajillos while catching a variety of sports events (especially a Canelo fight). Mariscos El Muelle 8 delivers a unique Sinaloan seafood experience as the only Mexico-based mariscos franchise in Los Angeles. What to order Tostada lovers are in for a treat. The tostada chavita — a very Sinaloan take on the popular tuna tostada — piles cubes of sweet and sour marinated tuna on a fried wonton, with a scattering of black sesame and a crown of crispy fried onions on top. It’s a little inspiration from the sushi bar that Sinaloan chefs learned in culinary school and working at sushi bars stateside. The tostada chavita is compact and leaves plenty of room for other dishes. The shrewdest scheme to get a taste of pricey callos de hacha (pen shell clams) is in an order of Ceviche Muelle 8 , a mix of cooked shrimp, raw shrimp, cooked octopus, and those prized callos de hacha in a medium spicy salsa roja. One of the hallmarks of any barra fría is a number of variations on aguachile, a dish consisting of raw, high-quality shrimp, cured à la minute in a spicy lime juice blended with chile serrano or chile jalapeño. Ordering an aguachile negro made with the restaurant’s umami-rich salsa negra is the move; pair it with a michelada. The best seafood taco selection in town announces itself with the Taco Gaxiola , a seared strip of tuna rubbed in adobo, topped with guacamole and pico de gallo, and dressed with a chipotle-mayo. Everything zarandeado is en vogue north of the border, and camarones zarandeados are a noteworthy plate on any barra caliente. Here, large shrimp are grilled in a spicy marinade and served with undressed salad and coleslaw. The vibe The roar of crowds and booming sportscaster voices transmitted on flat-screen televisions displaying rival matches reverberate off the walls and tavern-style ceiling. The nautical-themed dining room, white with navy blue trim, features a mural depicting a day at the beach in Sinaloa. Diners are casually dressed — snapbacks are a sharp accessory for young sinaloenses — and it’s best to come with friends or family to enjoy sharable ceviches, aguachiles, and botanas (snacks). Insider tip If you want spicier, just ask when you order dishes from the barra fría. And check out the shellfish behind the bar on your right as you walk in for the day’s selection, which can include pata de mula, reina, and chocolata clams as well as Pacific oysters. Tostada chavita at Mariscos El Muelle 8. items.title: With LA’s Bar Scene in Crisis, Everson Royce Bar Announces Last Call
items.summary: In late October, Downtown’s Everson Royce Bar announced it would close permanently at the end of 2026. Hundreds of comments on its Instagram page lamented the loss of another fundamental Los Angeles bar. In the 11 years it was open, Everson Royce Bar appealed to casual and knowledgeable drinkers alike, serving as a watering hole […]
items.text: LA Restaurant Closings With LA’s Bar Scene in Crisis, Everson Royce Bar Announces Last Call Co-owner Randy Clement says tourism is down, costs are up, and the entertainment workforce is staying home﻿ by Mona Holmes Nov 4, 2026, 11:51 PM UTC Facebook Link Everson Royce Bar in Arts District. Wonho Frank Lee Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. In late October, Downtown’s Everson Royce Bar announced it would close permanently at the end of 2026. Hundreds of comments on its Instagram page lamented the loss of another fundamental Los Angeles bar. In the 11 years it was open, Everson Royce Bar appealed to casual and knowledgeable drinkers alike, serving as a watering hole for the hospitality industry. Cocktail culture writer Esther Tseng recalls the bar’s impact on the region. “It’s a bar that always had seriously good (but not serious) cocktails,” says Tseng. “It was probably one of the first places I knew Downtown that could accommodate small parties in an intimate bar setting, or larger, casual parties on the patio out back. It had great food, too.” Partners Joe Capella, Randy Clement, April Langford, and chef Matt Molina debuted Everson Royce Bar in 2015 with an uncomplicated approach to cocktails, a selection of rare whiskeys, Molina’s notable cheeseburger and food menu , plus that welcoming outdoor area. The team brought plenty of experience from restaurants and bars across Southern California. Capella and Molina are longtime operators of Hippo and South Pasadena’s Cannonball , which opened in 2025. Wife-and-husband team Langford and Clement are the minds behind Good Neighbor Bar as well as West Altadena Wine, which the couple closed in October. Eater spoke to Clement about the reasoning behind his decision to shutter Everson Royce Bar and West Altadena Wine. Clement cited the same challenges other operators have in Los Angeles’s current business and consumer climate : a significant drop in tourism, rising operational costs, changing drinking trends, plus the long-term effects of the pandemic and entertainment industry strikes. This year has been one of the hardest for Southern California bars and nightlife. Clement sees businesses losing their customer base as the many film and television workers who have long fueled Los Angeles restaurants and bars — hospitality workers pursuing entertainment dreams with side gigs as well as higher-paid industry professionals — can no longer afford to go out to eat and drink regularly. “Closing Everson Royce was the perfect storm of everything going wrong at the same time,” says Clement. “But unless there is this other unnamed industry waiting in the wings to replace the industry that’s driven our town for the last decades upon decades, I’m concerned that there’s no looking back.” The foursome saw the numbers and had acknowledged the inevitable for some time. They extended the closure announcement to keep their workers employed, with a persistent optimism that conditions would improve. As for West Altadena Wine, which is attached to Good Neighbor Bar’s patio, Clement says he was unwilling to continue the lengthy conflict with a residential neighbor who allegedly targeted the business by complaining to government agencies like Los Angeles County’s Department of Public Works, Building and Safety, LA County Planning, and the Department of Public Health. Clement also says that the complainant called law enforcement before Langford and Clement finally closed West Altadena Wine in late October. Eater reached out to the complainant but did not hear back. Clement and Langford moved from Albuquerque, New Mexico, to Los Angeles in 1996. The couple currently resides in Altadena and, along with other Los Angeles operators, worries about business sustainability and the city’s culture. “Here in LA, anything is possible, and now it doesn’t feel like that,” says Clement. The year 2026 is proving challenging for Los Angeles nightlife. West Hollywood’s the Belmont shuttered in August, and the neighborhood’s renowned Employees Only closed in late September. On November 2, Augustine Wine Bar announced it will close on December 19, the same day as Everson Royce Bar. SF Gate reports that cocktail (and wings) favorite Ye Rustic Inn might lose its outdoor seating and cites lease concerns with the landlord. Owner Susan Wood hosted an event to bolster support for the almost 30-year-old bar, where Los Angeles mayoral candidate and councilmember Nithya Raman showed up to offer support for independent businesses. (As of this writing, one day after Election Day, Raman holds a small lead over incumbent Mayor Karen Bass.) Clement sees an emergency unfolding and hopes solutions can come from elected officials for all independent businesses. “If you’re the group formulating legislation for economic incentives or tax credits, the fact that this hasn’t happened yet, maybe it’s all too late,” says Clement. “I don’t know. What Everson Royce Bar is going through is what the florist, yoga studio, and bookstore are going through.” Everson Royce Bar Everson Royce Bar 1936 E 7th St, Los Angeles, CA, 90021, US Booking Book a table Phone (213) 335-6166 Link http://www.erbla.com/ See More : LA Restaurant Closings LA Restaurant News Cocktail Bars Most Popular The Best Restaurants in Palm Springs, According to Eater Editors The Best Los Angeles Restaurants for Thanksgiving Dinner The 18 Best Santa Monica Restaurants The 21 Best Indian and South Asian Restaurants in Los Angeles The Best Restaurants in Downtown Los Angeles, According to Eater Editors Advertiser Content From This is the title for the native ad

items.text: Coming Attractions Orange County Dining Juggernaut Kei Concepts Is Finally Expanding Into LA ﻿The restaurant group behind Vox Kitchen and Rol will anchor a massive new $24 million development in Culver City by Cathy Chaplin Nov 3, 2026, 11:05 PM UTC Facebook Link Wonho Frank Lee Cathy Chaplin is a former senior editor at Eater LA, a James Beard Award–nominated journalist, and the author of Food Lovers’ Guide to Los Angeles. What began 12 years ago as a single Buena Park pho shop has evolved into Kei Concepts , one of Orange County’s most dominant restaurant groups. Co-founded by James Beard-nominated chef Viet Nguyen, the group’s portfolio now spans nine unique brands — ranging from Italian-Japanese fusion to contemporary Chinese — across 14 locations and 1,200 employees. Next fall, Kei Concepts will make its move into Los Angeles, anchoring Culver Commons — a $24 million Regency Centers development at the intersection of Washington Boulevard and Centinela Avenue — with outposts of its Peruvian-Chinese staple Vox Kitchen and Japanese handroll counter Rol . (Kei Concepts operated Súp Noodle Bar in Cerritos from 2017 to 2020.) At Culver Commons, the two OC imports will join a stacked tenant lineup that includes Wanderlust Creamery, Smog City Brewing, and El Moro Churrería. While the partners behind Kei Concepts considered expanding beyond its Orange County “bubble” for years, Nguyen says, the group didn’t take the leap until Regency Centers approached them about the opportunity in Culver City. Previously, the two companies partnered at Heritage Plaza, an Irvine shopping complex owned by Regency Centers, where Kei Concepts operates three restaurants: Nếp Cafe, Súp Noodle Bar, and Rol Hand Roll Bar. “Culver City is the perfect location for our introduction of Kei Concepts to LA residents,” says Nguyen. He notes that the city’s demographics and income levels closely mirror those of the group’s most successful Orange County markets like Irvine, though with a smaller Asian population. Bringing Vox Kitchen to Los Angeles marks a full-circle moment for Nguyen. “When I was working all over LA, the number-one restaurant I always went to every single week was Mario’s Seafood,” he says. The long-standing Hollywood Peruvian restaurant’s signature ceviches and lomo saltado inspired Vox Kitchen. Vox Kitchen Culver City will seat 200 diners across a 5,000-square-foot dining room and a 1,000-square-foot patio, making it significantly larger than existing locations in Fountain Valley and South Coast Plaza. To further differentiate the restaurant from its predecessors, the Culver City menu is adding what Nguyen calls a “Nikkei flair” to its Chifa standards, introducing a raw bar and a dynamic slate of cocktails. Madrid-based architecture and experience firm Livit designed the restaurant’s sleek interiors. Three doors down, Rol, which currently operates in Fountain Valley, Irvine, and La Habra, will span 2,000 square feet, with counter-only seating. Its core menu of handrolls and donburi bowls will expand to feature a new lineup of traditional and innovative onigiri, including Korean-inspired variations like bulgogi and kimchi. Nguyen views the dual Culver City openings as a litmus test for the brand’s viability outside its home turf. “Culver City will be the defining moment,” Nguyen says. “If we open it and nobody shows up and they hate us, then we still have a lot of work to do. But if it succeeds and people love it, we’ll be in 50 states.” While it is too soon to say how the Orange County powerhouse will fare in a hyper-competitive market like Los Angeles’s, Nguyen’s underlying mission to foster connection within the Vietnamese diaspora through shared meals remains steadfast. “When you sit around the dinner table, everything becomes softer; you find it easier to forget. I feel like my job is to bring people together at the dinner table,” he says. “Everything I’m doing is for Little Saigon. Everything I’m doing is for Vietnamese people to come together to share stories.” Vox Culver City. Livit Vox Culver City. Elcielo Elcielo received a Michelin Star for its 18-course tasting menu by chef Juan Manuel Barrientos. The modern Colombian menu varies, but expect experiential moments like the restaurant’s “Tree of Life,” bread service entangled on a small tree; and the “Chocotherapy” which invites you to literally wash your hands in liquid cocoa. The tasting menu ranges from $245 to $289 per person (excluding beverages, tax, and a 20 percent added gratuity). Elcielo will accommodate people with allergies and offer a vegetarian menu upon request. There’s also a $98 bar experience where guests will experience a selection of cocktails, each paired with snacks. The restaurant is so intimate that it only accepts five guests at each of its seatings (there are two to three per evening). Those lucky enough to snag a coveted spot will experience Cory himself serving up the finest sushi flown in from Japan. The meal costs $280 per person (plus sake, a 20% service charge, and tax) and lasts approximately three hours. The menu is prepared specially each day, so substitutions are not allowed, and people with food allergies cannot be accommodated. items.text: Tin Tin Dining Out in Miami The Best New Bars in Miami Where to grab a drink right now in the Magic City by Allison Ramirez Updated Jul 15, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Allison Ramirez is a freelance journalist with over 15 years of experience covering food and drink, travel, art, culture, and more. As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping the city’s evolving cocktail landscape. Miami’s drinking culture really reflects its melting pot history, and this year, some iconic bars and restaurants have reopened with a refreshed look and feel, bringing back old-school favorites alongside international, travel-inspired drinks. From tiki recipes and passion fruit infusions to sparkling concoctions of all sorts, our latest cocktail map highlights the best drinks and the hottest new spots to try them, from Coral Gables to Miami Beach and everywhere in between. items.summary: A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. items.text: Austin Restaurant News Fire-Grilled Mexican Seafood Is Coming to South Austin The team behind Roya and Oasthouse will open Mi Vecino, a coastal restaurant focused on raw and fire-kissed dishes by Erin Russell Oct 28, 2026, 6:47 PM UTC Facebook Link Chef Amir Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, managed by Mi Vecino’s executive chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. Sarah Natsumi Moore/Eater Erin Russell is a journalist and an Austin native, who has been writing about food for eight years. A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen , which closed Saturday, October 24. Mi Vecino, which means my neighbor in Spanish, will focus on Mexican seafood dishes, both raw and fire-grilled. That means offerings like shrimp enchiladas with white mole, ceviche, oysters, and fajitas served with fresh tortillas. Drinks-wise, there will be a full bar with margaritas, ranch waters, palomas, and other cocktails. Chef Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, which will be executed by chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. The Hajimalekis’ restaurants are mostly clustered on Slaughter Lane in South Austin. Gastropub Oasthouse Kitchen + Bar , cocktail bar Daisy Lounge , and forthcoming Mi Vecino all share a building, and the group’s first restaurant , American spot District Kitchen + Cocktails , is just down the street. Mi Vecino replaces Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen, a different Roya Hospitality Group restaurant that closed in October. Jasmin Porter Photography This is not the first time Roya Hospitality Group has reimagined one of their restaurants. Roya , Hajimalekis’ highly personal Persian restaurant in North Shoal Creek, opened this year in a space that was previously Shortie’s, the group’s foray into New England Greek-style pizza. Roya is the group’s only North Austin restaurant, and sits above a former second District Kitchen, which closed and became an event space. Given the group’s penchant for reinvention, only time will tell whether it stays an event space. Whether you’re planning a milestone birthday, hosting a corporate dinner, or gathering friends for an engagement celebration, Austin has a private dining room to suit your needs. Some are swanky and tucked into Downtown dining landmarks. Others are cozy, or perched on patios with sweeping views. All of them make an outing feel like an event, while also taking the stress out of group dining — meaning, there’s no awkward table shuffling, no shouting over the crowd, and no fighting for the check. The city’s best private dining spaces are more than just a curtain and a prix fixe menu. Many spots go beyond dinner, offering perks like custom cocktails, floral design, built-in audio and video setups, and after-hours buyouts. From iconic institutions like Fonda San Miguel, Matties, and Jeffrey’s to sleek hotspots like Eberly, La Condessa, and Bar Toti, these venues combine atmosphere with standout service and memorable menus. items.title: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques
items.summary:
At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla… 
 The post  Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Cotoletta’s Only Entree Honors Italian Traditions and Age-Old Techniques — Resy | Right This Way Cotoletta 4.7 · Italian · $ Miami Book Now Published: Nov. 9, 2026 At Cotoletta in Coconut Grove, there are no decisions to make. The Miami restaurant serves only one entree: Cotoletta alla Milanese. No substitutions. No alternatives. Just a golden, pan-fried veal cutlet — and a bet that it’s all you’ll need. Until recently, making a reservation required a phone call, which only deepened the sense that this place operates on its own terms. (The good news: You can now reserve a table on Resy.) The concept debuted in Coconut Grove in the fall of 2024 and comes from 84 Magic Hospitality, a restaurant group known for a growing collection of Miami restaurants with minimalist menus ( San Lorenzo , San Marco , and the lasagna speakeasy, Si Papa 3190 , are the others). Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Still, the story behind the concept stretches back further than its Miami address might suggest. Cotoletta is the creation of partners Ignacio Lopez Mancisidor and Mattia Cicognani, and former co-founder Andrea Fraquelli — who share a background in hospitality and a frustration with how transactional the industry had become. From the start, their goal at Cotoletta has been to make things simple for guests and allow them to focus on what really matters: great food and genuine connection. “Across the globe, many of the best restaurants do one item and they do it to absolute perfection,” co-founder Mattia Cicognani says. “We drew inspiration from the Italian essence of committing to one hero dish and prioritizing ingredients of the highest quality.” “Only serving one dish was a risk,” Cicognani acknowledges, “but the popularity and love for the concept has proven that it really works. Our customers learned that they love what we do and that is why they continue to come back.” Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Photo courtesy of Cotoletta Head chef Davide Rosselli shared the process that delivers a consistent, classic cotoletta every time. Premium veal is hand-trimmed, gently pounded to its thin-yet-tender texture, coated in fresh egg and breadcrumbs, and fried in clarified butter until it emerges with a crisp, even, golden crust. Each cutlet weighs in at roughly 20 ounces, made to be shared between two people. The result is a traditional veal Milanese that is a signature of Northern Italian craftsmanship. Everything else on the table exists to support that centerpiece. “While the process sounds simple, it’s backed by decades of Italian tradition and time-honored techniques passed down by chefs across generations,” Rosselli says. For $90, two diners share the full prix-fixe experience: two antipasti courses of bruschetta and truffle arancino to start, followed by the veal cutlet, and two sides (the only real choice you have to make here). Dessert (tiramisu or a flourless chocolate cake) can be added on for $14. “Each appetizer sets the tone for a true Italian experience, while the sides are thoughtfully chosen to complement the veal without overpowering it.” Rosselli says. “Lighter elements like crisp salads and simple pasta dishes help balance the richness of the veal, creating a well-rounded meal.” Those side options include pasta al pomodoro, zucchine fritte, insalata di rucola, or patatine fritte. Rosselli’s personal picks: the pasta in just the right portion to leave you wanting more of the main event, and the zucchine fritte offering a warm, light bite that balances out the richness of the veal. (Wondering what happens if you bring a third wheel or want to dine solo? Odd-numbered parties can add on an individual portion of bruschetta, arancino, a smaller veal cutlet, and one side for $55.) Guests return because the menu never changes, and neither does the reason to go back. “They know exactly what they are getting every single time,” Cicognani says. Cotoletta is open weekdays from 5:30 to 10 p.m. and until 10:30 p.m. on Friday. On weekends, it opens at 12:30 p.m. until 10:30 p.m. on Saturday and 9 p.m. on Sunday. Lyssa Goldberg is a Miami-based freelance writer and content strategist. She loves telling stories about food, wellness and travel, and you can find her byline in Parade, American Way, Mashable, Miami New Times, Time Out and more. Follow her on Instagram and Twitter . Follow Resy , too. items.text: The Resy Guide to Bars and Restaurants for Music Lovers in New York — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 As people who love restaurants, we know that when it comes to picking a spot for dinner, it’s much more than about just the food. The vibe is just as important, and music is a key player in creating it. Sometimes, the best soundtrack is the one you don’t notice, but the places on this list aren’t for those kinds of nights. These playlists are hyper specific, the sound systems are top of the line, and often they have some of the best vinyl collections in the country, and a guest DJs on weekends who comes in to spin them. These are places you go to for the music, but where us restaurant lovers won’t need to suffer because the snacks that can often lead to full meals are far more interesting than a bag of stale potato chips. You’ll be able to listen to some Japanese jazz deep cuts over an omakase, or eclectic world beats over some of the city’s silkiest hummus — with playlists and menus like these, you might not need to make it to your second destination for the night. And if you’re looking for spots with live music, we’ve got you covered here . Wine Hit List The NYC Wine Hit List, Summer 2025 Edition: Lei, Borgo, Bar Tizio, and More By Vicki Denig and Jon Bonné Today 2 Close Party Size Remove 2 Add Update Close Date 56709 map Long Island City Photo courtesy of 56709 What was once 929, an audio haven for Canto pop, is now a moody, atmospheric spot for Japanese city pop, from the same team. You’ll also find plenty of records that include J-pop from the 90s and 2000s, plus Japanese R&B. And the theme isn’t strictly limited to the music, either. Cocktails are named after Japanese pop stars (Anri, Momoko, Ryuichi) and anime (Agumon, Usagi), and food is a fusion of Japanese and Taiwanese flavors: Think radish cakes with XO sauce, braised pork over rice, and mala-seasoned French fries. Book Now Birds map West Village Whether you’re partial to live music or listening bar vibes, Birds has you covered. On weeknights they spin selections from their enormous vinyl collection, and on weekends they host live musicians in a variety of styles like ska, jazz, and Afrobeats. Know that on Fridays and Saturdays there’s a $30 cover charge, but it’s a small price to pay for the incredible night of music that you’re in for. Book Now Boro Brine map Williamsburg The bar. Photo by Ben Hon, courtesy of Boro Brine There are two concepts at this Williamsburg restaurant, an intimate 22-seat omakase counter and a Japanese-inspired cocktail bar. Audiophiles will be satisfied at either, as music runs throughout and the sound system is top notch. The chef’s tasting consists of an ever-changing menu of multiple courses for $98 a person, whereas the bar has an à la carte menu that features inventive cocktails and bites like a chef’s take on a filet-o-fish and octopus with saag paneer. With velvet banquets and a dimly lit interior, it’s also a perfect date night spot. Book Now ALL BLUES map Tribeca Photo courtesy of All Blues Don’t be surprised if you’re asked to keep quiet at this Tribeca listening room. It’s all about the music here, so much so to that conversation is discouraged. All Blues comes from owner Yuji Fukushima, who based the concept on the places he frequented back growing up in Tokyo. He’s invested in top-tier audio equipment and carefully selects the music each evening, which can range from funk to Dizzy Gillespie. Enjoy Japanese snacks like tempura sweet potatoes and gyoza, alongside a fine whiskey or sake while you take in the sounds. Book Now Record Room map Long Island City Photo courtesy of Record Room This Long Island City bar might be a little hard to find at first, but that’s the idea. Behind a hidden door, you’ll be transported to a music filled living room of sorts, filled with comfy couches and soft lighting. All the music here is played off vinyl and there might be occasional dancing. The drinks lean classic, with riffs on espresso martinis

items.text: 29 New York Bars and Restaurants with Excellent Zero-Proof Cocktails — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 9, 2026 Somewhere around a decade ago the dreaded term “mocktail” first started to surface on menus, referring to drinks meant to offer the cocktail experience, but none of the “buzz.” At the time, unlike their alcoholic counterparts, most of these drinks were overly sweet mixes of juice and housemade sodas with elaborate garnishes. Now, however, there’s been a shift in drinking culture: Dry January, anyone? In other words, we’re drinking less, or thinking about having that second or third drink more, and beverage directors have taken note. Today’s mocktails are now as considered and thoughtfully developed as those made full-strength. Many of them also feature the new wave of non-alcoholic spirits, like Seedlip, Lyre’s, Little Saints, Amass Riverine, and Ghia. So, whether you’re abstaining from alcohol, are taking a night off, or just want to stay and linger at the bar after your glass has run dry, here are some of the best places in the city to find zero-proof cocktails. Newly added: Bar Americano, Lord’s, Overstory, and The Up & Up. Party Size Remove 2 Add Update Close Date Soft Bar + Cafe map Greenpoint One of the newer additions to the non-alcoholic cocktail scene in our fair city, Soft Bar is so named because all of the drinks on their all-day menu are, well, soft. The Golden Hour , with grape, elderflower, pink peppercorn shrub, and alcohol-free Champagne, or the Pear Pressure with prickly pear, agave, and alcohol-free Tequila, are both good choices. Keep an eye out on the menu for the function of each drink, which ranges from focus to “vibey.” Plus, there’s a celebrity at the helm – fans of Bravo’s Summer House might see a familiar face. Read all about Soft Bar here . Book Now Golden Ratio map Clinton Hill What can’t this team do? Golden Ratio comes from the masterminds behind Cafe Mado and Place des Fêtes , serving up cocktails and mocktails to the Clinton Hill crowd. Nearly all of the cocktails here have a nonalcoholic counterpart, and everything is fiercely flavor-driven and seasonal. Past drinks have included interpretations of purple shiso , apple , and toothache tree , and the team is working towards being zero-waste, so you can have your drink and eat it, too. Book Now Lord's map NoHo This beloved purveyor of British fare may not be the first thing that comes to mind when you think of nonalcoholic beverages, but their list (which they title “Teetotaling”) is one of our favorites. Go for a Blood Orange Spritz , a sour made with Ghia, or a S affron White Negroni — all totally alcohol free, of course. Any of them pairs perfectly with a good lamb Scotch egg, too. Book Now Sofreh map Prospect Heights There’s not a lot we’d say no to at Sofreh. While yes, their list of cocktails is excellent, the real pearl here has to be the selection of sharbats , a Persian cooler that comes in flavors like mint and cucumber, sour cherry, and lemon and saffron. If those aren’t doing it for you, there’s also the Persian black tea and a mint and rose petal yogurt drink. No matter what’s in your glass, make sure an order of herb meatballs and saffron rice are on your table. Book Now The Up & Up map Greenwich Village This subterranean cocktail den and ideal date night spot in Greenwich Village has an extensive list of drinks that also includes five excellent nonalcoholic takes on some of their classics. This includes a zero-proof spin of Hold, Please , a watermelon shrub that draws inspiration from New York’s sliced fruit vendors who often sell servings of watermelon spears topped with Tajín. There’s also an N/A version of Zuzu’s Petals , named for the classic film, “It’s a Wonderful Life,” that’s made with ginger, habanero, rose water, lime juice, and demerara. Book Now Spygold map Hudson Yards Greywind’s (also on this list) sister and downstairs neighbor, the fire-lit Spygold, has an equally lovely list of non-alcoholic options for you to peruse. Past favorites have included the Tomato, Tomahto with nonalcoholic gin and tomato-basil soda, or the Cucumber Highball with alcohol-free Tequila and cucumber soda. items.title: The Ultimate Resy Guide to Splurge-Worthy Dining in Miami
items.summary:
Miami offers plenty of chances to spend big bucks on dinner, but the harder question is where to make it… 
 The post  The Ultimate Resy Guide to Splurge-Worthy Dining in Miami  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: Amazonico Miami map Brickell Come dressed for dinner and whatever follows at Amazónico, where live bands play jazz, bossa nova, and Cuban rhythms beneath a canopy of greenery. The menu is as extravagant as the setting: guacamole comes topped with sea urchin, and Maine lobster tail arrives with semolina pasta and coconut bisque. Share ceviche with sweet plantain and duck arroz chaufa before moving on to charcoal-grilled picanha or Australian wagyu ribeye. After dinner, follow the music upstairs, where DJs and tropical cocktails keep the lounge and rooftop going into the wee hours of the night. Photo courtesy of Amazónico Miami Cost: A meal for two, including drinks, will likely cost more than $125 per person. Starters range in price from $13 to $42, nigiri sushi is $45 to $65, sashimi is $60 to $80, seafood entrees are priced from $32 to $110, and grilled meats are $38 to $380 each. Book Now
